And like any discipline, the more you practice it, the more natural, and the more powerful, it becomes.

books.pt: Tenha mais confiança nas interações sociais
paras: Vanessa Van Edwards describes herself as a recovering awkward person. She wasn't a natural at social situations — she found them baffling and anxiety-inducing — so she did something characteristically nerdy about it: she started treating human behavior as a science to be studied. She founded a research lab called Science of People, where she runs experiments on charisma, body language, and influence, and in Captivate she distills that research into a practical, evidence-based playbook. Her core promise is that people skills aren't an innate gift. They're a set of hackable, learnable techniques — you can study interaction the way you'd study chemistry, and get predictably better at it.

Van Edwards organizes the book around the natural phases of a relationship, which gives it a clear structure: the first five minutes, the first five hours, and the first five days. The first five minutes are about first impressions and how to work a room. The first five hours are about decoding people and understanding what makes them tick. And the first five days are about building a lasting connection. It's a useful map, because the skills you need to make a great first impression are different from the ones you need to deepen a relationship over time.

Let's start with the first five minutes. One of her most practical ideas is to stop relying on boring small talk — because "What do you do?" and "How are you?" produce boring, autopilot answers that make you forgettable. Instead, she teaches conversation sparks: opener questions engineered to trigger a little hit of dopamine, the brain's reward and novelty chemical. Questions like "What was the highlight of your day?" or "Working on anything exciting lately?" These pull people out of their scripted responses and light them up, and — crucially — Van Edwards points to research suggesting that when you produce dopamine during a conversation, you don't just make the exchange more enjoyable, you actually make yourself more memorable. The person associates the good feeling with you.

She's also strategic about where you socialize. She encourages you to know your thrive locations versus your survive locations — the settings where you're energized and at your best, versus the ones that drain you. If big loud parties make you shrink, stop forcing yourself to network at them and choose environments where you naturally shine, like smaller gatherings or one-on-one coffees. Play the social game on your home turf. And within any room, she offers a simple navigation tip: head for the social zone — the open, productive middle of the room — rather than lingering by the entrance or hiding near the bar.

In the first five hours, the focus shifts to decoding people, and here Van Edwards brings in some genuinely fascinating science. She teaches readers to recognize the seven universal microexpressions — the fleeting facial expressions that flash across everyone's face, in every culture, revealing true emotion: anger, fear, surprise, disgust, contempt, happiness, and sadness. Learning to catch these gives you a kind of emotional radar, letting you notice what someone really feels even when their words say otherwise. She also introduces the Big Five personality traits — openness, conscientiousness, extroversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism — as a framework for speed-reading the people around you, so you can adjust your approach to fit who they actually are rather than treating everyone the same.

Another memorable concept is what she calls being a highlighter. A highlighter is someone who constantly looks for the good in others and reflects it back to them. When you tell people what's great about them, she says, they actually become better, and they associate that elevated feeling with you. This connects to a well-documented psychological phenomenon she draws on called the Ben Franklin effect — the counterintuitive finding that when someone does you a small favor, or you ask them for advice or help, they tend to like you more, not less. A little vulnerability, a small request for help, builds connection rather than diminishing you.

For the first five days and building lasting connection, Van Edwards teaches a technique she calls story stacking. Rather than being caught flat when someone asks "So what's new?", you prepare a small arsenal of go-to stories triggered by common topics, built with a hook, a bit of struggle, and a memorable detail — and then you use what she calls the boomerang, bouncing the conversation back to the other person so they become the star and feel valued. Underneath it all is a principle she states plainly: don't try to impress people — engage them. The goal is never to perform at someone; it's to make them feel interesting, understood, and important.

So the actionable takeaways: replace generic small talk with two or three conversation sparks, like "What was the highlight of your day?", to trigger dopamine and become memorable. Spend your social energy in your thrive locations rather than forcing yourself where you struggle. Learn the seven microexpressions so you can read what people truly feel, and roughly place people on the Big Five so you can tailor your approach. Be a highlighter, actively naming the good in others. And use the Ben Franklin effect — ask for small favors and show a little vulnerability — to deepen liking.

What makes Captivate distinctive is its blend of hard behavioral science and immediately usable tactics. Van Edwards isn't asking you to become a different, more extroverted person. She's giving you the underlying rules of social interaction — the patterns and triggers that were always operating beneath the surface — and showing you how to work with them deliberately. For anyone who has ever felt that other people seemed to have a secret social instruction manual they never received, this book is essentially that manual, written by someone who had to figure it all out from scratch, and who proves that the skills of connection can be learned by anyone willing to study them.

books.pt: Lide com conversas difíceis com confiança
books.a: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton & Sheila Heen
paras: Some conversations we genuinely dread — telling an employee their work isn't good enough, confronting a friend who let us down, raising a grievance with a partner, saying no to someone we don't want to disappoint. Difficult Conversations, written by Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton, and Sheila Heen of the Harvard Negotiation Project — the same group that produced the negotiation classic Getting to Yes — is the definitive guide to handling exactly these moments. Drawing on decades of research into negotiation and communication, the authors argue that difficult conversations, as varied as they seem, all share a hidden structure. And once you understand that structure, you can navigate them with far less anxiety and much better results.

Their central discovery is that every difficult conversation is actually three conversations happening at once. Most of us only pay attention to the surface one, and that's why these talks so often go badly.

The first is what they call the "What Happened?" conversation. This is the disagreement over facts — what's true, what was said, who's right, and who's to blame. We tend to assume difficult conversations are fights about the facts. But the authors make a crucial point: they're rarely really about the facts. They're about conflicting perceptions, interpretations, and values. You and the other person are each certain you see the situation clearly, but you're actually operating from different stories, built from different information and different assumptions. The trap here is what they call the battle of messages — each side trying to prove they're right and the other is wrong. The way out is to move from a stance of certainty to a stance of curiosity: to get genuinely interested in how the other person sees things, rather than assuming your version is the truth.

The second conversation is the "Feelings" conversation. Difficult conversations are, at their core, almost always emotional — and yet we usually try to keep feelings out of them, treating emotions as an inconvenient distraction from the "real" issue. The authors insist this is backwards. Feelings are usually at the very heart of the matter, and if you don't address them, they don't disappear — they leak out sideways, as sarcasm, as a sharp tone, as withdrawal, poisoning the whole exchange. Part of the work, then, is to sort out what you're actually feeling, often buried beneath layers of judgment and blame, and to express those feelings clearly rather than acting them out.

The third conversation is the subtlest and often the most powerful: the "Identity" conversation. This is the conversation you have with yourself, about what the situation means for your self-image. Am I competent, or am I a fraud? Am I a good person, or a bad one? Am I worthy of love? Difficult conversations threaten our identity, and that's why they make us so anxious — a piece of critical feedback can feel like an attack on our whole sense of who we are. The authors offer a remedy they call grounding your identity, or adopting an "and stance." The problem, they explain, is all-or-nothing thinking — I'm either perfect or worthless. The solution is to complexify your self-image: to accept that you can be a skilled professional and have made a real mistake, that you can be a good person and have hurt someone. When your identity is more complex and resilient, feedback stops feeling like an existential threat, and you can actually hear it.

With that three-part map in hand, the book offers a toolkit for having these conversations well. One of the most valuable tools is what they call the Third Story. When you open a difficult conversation, don't lead with your version of events, because that immediately puts the other person on the defensive. Instead, describe the problem the way a neutral third party — an impartial observer watching from the outside — would describe it, in a way that captures the gap between the two perspectives without judging either. "It seems like you and I see this project's problems very differently" is a third story. "You dropped the ball on this project" is not. The third story invites collaboration instead of triggering a fight.

Another essential distinction is between intent and impact. Here's the trap the authors identify: we judge ourselves by our intentions, but we judge others by their impact on us. So when someone's actions hurt us, we leap to the conclusion that they intended to hurt us — even though, if the roles were reversed, we'd want them to know our own bad impact came from good or neutral intentions. The discipline is to separate the two: acknowledge the impact something had on you, but don't assume you know the other person's intent. Ask about it instead. That single shift defuses an enormous amount of conflict.

Related to this is their move from blame to contribution. Blame is backward-looking and about judgment — whose fault is this? — and it makes everyone defensive and shuts down learning. Contribution is different: instead of asking who's to blame, you ask how each of us contributed to the situation we're now in. Almost always, both parties contributed something, and mapping that honestly, without blame, opens the door to actually fixing the problem. As the authors put it, focusing on blame inhibits our ability to learn what's really causing the problem.

Underneath all of these tools is one overarching shift: moving from what they call the battle of messages to a learning conversation. Instead of entering the conversation to deliver your verdict and win, you enter it to learn — to understand the other person's story, share your own, and jointly figure out what to do. You still say what you need to say, clearly and honestly. But you hold your view and stay curious about theirs at the same time.

So the takeaways: before any hard conversation, walk yourself through all three conversations — sort out the facts and your assumptions, name your feelings, and notice what identity issue is at stake for you. Open with the third story, framing the problem as a neutral observer would. Trade certainty for curiosity about how the other person sees it. Separate intent from impact — describe the impact, but ask about the intent rather than assuming the worst. Move from blame to contribution. And ground your own identity so feedback doesn't feel like an attack.

The lasting wisdom of Difficult Conversations is that these dreaded exchanges don't have to be battles to be won or lost. They can be, instead, opportunities to understand and be understood. The authors are honest that this approach won't magically produce agreement every time. But it will make the conversation more honest, less combative, and far more likely to preserve the relationship — which, in the end, is usually what matters most.
Chapter 1. The Man Nobody Wanted.
A man walked into a small town. He was tired and hungry. His clothes were old. His face was hard.

His name was Jean Valjean. He had just come out of prison. He was in prison for nineteen years. Why? Because, long ago, he was poor and hungry. He stole one piece of bread for his sister's children. Then he tried to run away many times. So the years grew and grew.
Now he was free. But freedom was not good.
He came to an inn. "I want food and a bed," he said. "I can pay."
"No," said the man at the inn. "We know who you are. Go away."
Everywhere it was the same. No one gave him food. No one gave him a bed. People saw the word "prison" on his face. They were afraid of him. They sent him away.
Night came. It was cold. Jean Valjean sat on a stone in the street. His heart was full of anger.
"I am not a man to them," he thought. "I am a dog."
Chapter 2. The Silver.
A woman saw him. "Go to that house," she said. "Knock on the door."
Jean Valjean knocked. An old man opened the door. He was the Bishop — a good and kind churchman.
"Come in," the Bishop said. "You are hungry. Sit. Eat with me."
Jean Valjean could not believe it. "But I come from prison," he said. "Do you know that?"
"I know," said the Bishop. "Sit down. You are my brother tonight."
They ate together with the Bishop's fine silver plates and cups. Then the Bishop gave Jean Valjean a good bed.

But in the night, Jean Valjean woke up. He looked at the silver. It was worth a lot of money. His old life was still inside him. Quietly, he took the silver, put it in his bag, and ran away into the dark.
In the morning, the police caught him. They brought him back to the Bishop.
"This man says you gave him this silver," the police said. "Is it true?"
Jean Valjean waited. Now he would go back to prison forever.
But the Bishop smiled. "Yes, I gave it to him," he said. "My friend, you forgot the silver candlesticks. I gave you those too. Take them."
The police let Jean Valjean go.
When they were alone, the Bishop spoke softly. "Jean Valjean, you are not a bad man now. I have bought your soul with this silver. Use it to become an honest man. Promise me."
Jean Valjean could not speak. His whole body shook. Something broke open inside him. For the first time in many years, he cried.
That day, Jean Valjean became a new man.
Chapter 3. The Good Mayor.
Years passed.

In another town, there was a rich, kind man. He owned a big factory. He gave work to poor people. He gave money to the sick. Everyone loved him. They made him the mayor. His name was Monsieur Madeleine.
But this was a secret: Monsieur Madeleine was Jean Valjean. He had changed his name and started a new life. He kept his promise to the Bishop. He was good to everyone.
In his town lived a police inspector. His name was Javert. Javert was cold and hard. He believed in the law, and only the law. To Javert, a criminal was always a criminal, forever.
Javert looked at the mayor. Something about him felt wrong. "I have seen this man before," Javert thought. "A long time ago. In a prison."
But he was not sure. So he watched, and he waited.
Chapter 4. Fantine.
A young woman worked in Monsieur Madeleine's factory. Her name was Fantine.

Fantine had a big secret and a broken heart. She had a little daughter, but no husband. The father had left them. Fantine had no money to keep her child with her. So she sent her daughter to live with an innkeeper and his wife — the Thénardiers — in another town. Every month she sent them money for the child.
The little girl's name was Cosette.
But the Thénardiers were cruel and greedy. They made Cosette work like a servant. She was cold, hungry, and sad. And they always asked Fantine for more and more money.
One day, the other women at the factory learned Fantine's secret. "She has a child and no husband!" they said. They were unkind. The factory boss sent Fantine away. Now she had no work.

Fantine was desperate. Cosette needed money. So Fantine sold her hair. Then she sold her teeth. Then, at last, she sold herself on the streets. She did terrible things to feed her child. She grew thin and ill.
She did not know that the kind mayor was the owner of the factory that had sent her away.
Chapter 5. A Promise.
One cold night, Fantine was sick and could not stand. The police wanted to take her away. Javert was there.
But the mayor came. Monsieur Madeleine looked at Fantine's sad, thin face. His heart hurt.
"Let her go," he said. "This poor woman is not a criminal. She is a mother. I will take care of her."
He took Fantine to a hospital. He sat by her bed.
"Where is my Cosette?" Fantine cried. "I want my child!"
"Do not be afraid," Monsieur Madeleine said gently. "I will bring her to you. I promise."
Fantine smiled a little. For the first time in a long time, she felt hope.
Javert watched all this. His cold eyes grew narrow. He did not understand this soft heart. To him, it looked weak, and it looked suspicious.
Chapter 6. The Terrible Choice.
Then Javert came to the mayor with strange news.
"Sir," Javert said, "I made a mistake. I thought you were an old prisoner named Jean Valjean. But I was wrong. The real Jean Valjean is caught. He is another man. He will go to prison tomorrow."
Monsieur Madeleine went cold.
Another man! An innocent man was going to prison in his place. If Madeleine said nothing, he was safe forever. He could keep his money, his good name, and his promise to Fantine.
But it was a lie. And the lie would destroy an innocent life.
All night, Jean Valjean fought with himself. His new life or the truth? His freedom or another man's life?
In the morning, he made his choice.
He went to the court where the innocent man stood. He stood up in front of everyone.
"Stop," he said. "This man is not Jean Valjean. I am Jean Valjean."
The room was silent. People could not believe it. The great, good mayor was an old prisoner.
Jean Valjean had saved a stranger. But now the law would come for him.
Chapter 7. Fantine's Last Breath.
Jean Valjean hurried back to the hospital, to Fantine.
But he was too late for peace. Javert came into the room. His face was hard and happy. "You are under arrest," Javert said. "You are only a prisoner. There is no mayor here."
Fantine heard these words. She looked at the kind man and the cruel policeman. She was so weak, so frightened.
"Cosette..." she whispered. "My child..."
And then Fantine died.
Jean Valjean's heart broke. He looked at Javert with terrible sadness. "You have killed her," he said quietly.
Javert took him away. But Jean Valjean was strong. Soon he escaped from Javert's hands. He had one thing to do now, one promise to keep.
He had to find Cosette.
Chapter 8. Cosette.
Jean Valjean traveled to the town of the Thénardiers.
It was night, and cold. In the dark forest, he saw a small child. She was carrying a heavy bucket of water. She was too little for such heavy work. Her feet were bare. She was crying quietly.
It was Cosette.
Jean Valjean took the heavy bucket. "Let me carry that," he said softly. "Whose child are you?"
Cosette told him about the inn, about the cruel people, about her hard life.

Jean Valjean went to the inn. The Thénardiers wanted money — a lot of money — before they would let the child go. Jean Valjean paid them. Then he took Cosette by the hand and walked away into the night.
For the first time, Cosette had someone who was kind. And for the first time in his lonely life, Jean Valjean had someone to love, like a daughter.
They went to the big city of Paris. They found a quiet place to live. They were happy and safe.
But they had to hide. Because somewhere in the city, Inspector Javert was always looking.
Chapter 9. Cosette and Marius.
Many years passed. Cosette grew up. She was young and beautiful and kind. Jean Valjean loved her like his own child, and she loved him like a father.
One day, in a park, Cosette met a young man. His name was Marius. He was a poor student with a good heart. Cosette and Marius looked at each other, and they fell in love.
But Jean Valjean was afraid. He did not want to lose Cosette. And he had to keep his secret hidden. So he kept them apart.

At this time, there was trouble in Paris. Many poor and angry people wanted to fight the government. Young students, like Marius, built a barricade in the street — a big wall of wood, stones, and furniture. They were ready to fight and to die.
Marius went to the barricade. He thought his life with Cosette was impossible. He did not care if he died.
Jean Valjean learned that Marius was at the barricade. He knew Cosette loved this young man. So, for her, he went too — into the middle of the fighting.
Chapter 10. The Barricade and the River.
The fighting was terrible. Guns fired. Men fell. The barricade was going to fall.
At the barricade, Jean Valjean found something surprising: Javert. The police had sent Javert as a spy, and the students had caught him. They wanted to kill him.
"Let me do it," Jean Valjean said.
He took Javert away, behind a wall, alone. Javert waited to die. He had chased this man for years.
But Jean Valjean did not kill him. He cut the ropes. "Go," he said. "You are free."
Javert could not understand. His enemy had saved his life.
Then the soldiers attacked. Many students died. Marius was shot and badly hurt. He fell, almost dead.
Jean Valjean picked him up. He carried Marius down into the sewers — the dark, dirty tunnels under the city. It was long and terrible. But Jean Valjean was strong, and he did not stop.
At last he came out. And there stood Javert.
"Take me," Jean Valjean said. "But first, help me take this young man home. He is hurt. Please."

Javert looked at the man who had saved his life. His whole world was breaking. The law said: arrest this criminal. But his heart said: this man is good. Javert could not live with these two truths together.
He let Jean Valjean go. Then Javert walked to the river. He looked at the dark water for a long time. And then he jumped in. Javert was gone.
Chapter 11. The Last Days.
Marius got well. He and Cosette married. It was a happy day.

But Jean Valjean was tired and old now. He told Marius his secret: that he was once a prisoner. He was afraid it would hurt Cosette's new life. So, quietly, sadly, he went away from them. He did not want to bring shame to Cosette.
Jean Valjean lived alone. Every day, he grew weaker. He missed Cosette so much. He was dying of a broken heart.
But then Marius learned the truth. He learned that Jean Valjean was the man who saved his life in the sewers. He learned that this "criminal" was the best man he had ever known.
Marius and Cosette ran to Jean Valjean's little room. They found the old man near the end of his life.
"Father!" Cosette cried. She took his hands.
Jean Valjean smiled. His eyes were full of tears and joy. His child had come back to him.
"Cosette," he said softly. "I loved you so much. Be happy. Love each other. That is the only thing that matters in this life."
He looked toward the Bishop's silver candlesticks. They still stood by his bed. He had kept them all these years. Their light shone on his face.
And then, peaceful and loved at last, Jean Valjean closed his eyes and died.
He came from prison, hated by all. He became a good man, loved by all. And in the end, that love was enough.
The End.
Chapter 1. A Happy Young Man.
Edmond Dantès was a young sailor. He was nineteen years old. He was kind, honest, and good at his job.
One day, his ship came home to the French city of Marseille. Everything in Edmond's life was going well.
His captain had died on the journey, so the ship's owner, a good man named Monsieur Morrel, wanted to give Edmond a big reward. "You will be the new captain," Morrel said.
Edmond was very happy. He was going to be a captain, young and successful.
And there was more. Edmond was in love. Her name was Mercédès, and she was beautiful and kind. She loved Edmond too. They were going to marry very soon.
Edmond had a good job, a woman he loved, and a bright future. He thought his life was perfect.
But some people were watching him, and they were not happy for him. They were jealous.
Chapter 2. Three Jealous Men.
Three men did not like Edmond's happiness.
The first was Danglars. He worked on the same ship. He wanted to be captain himself, and he hated that Edmond got the job instead.
The second was Fernand. He was in love with Mercédès. He wanted to marry her. He hated Edmond because Mercédès loved Edmond, not him.
These two men made a wicked plan. They wrote a secret letter. The letter said a lie: that Edmond was a dangerous traitor to France, an enemy of the country.
A third weak man, a neighbour, knew about the plan but did nothing to stop it.
The letter went to the police. Now Edmond was in terrible danger, and he did not even know it.
Chapter 3. Arrested at the Wedding.
It was Edmond's wedding day. He and Mercédès stood together with their friends and family. There was food, music, and laughter. Everyone was celebrating.
Then the door opened. Soldiers came in.
"Edmond Dantès," they said, "you are under arrest."
Everyone was shocked. Mercédès cried. Edmond did not understand.
"There is a mistake," Edmond said. "I have done nothing wrong."
The soldiers took him to a judge named Villefort. Villefort read the secret letter. He looked at Edmond's honest face, and he began to think that Edmond really was innocent.

But then Villefort saw a name in the case — a name that could destroy his own family and his career. To protect himself, Villefort decided to hide the truth. He chose to send an innocent man to prison to save himself.
"Take him away," Villefort said.
Edmond was thrown into a boat and taken far out to sea, to a terrible prison on a rock in the water. It was called the Château d'If. No one ever came back from there.
The door of a dark, cold cell closed behind him. Edmond was alone.
Chapter 4. The Years Pass.
Edmond stayed in the dark prison for a long, long time.
At first, he cried and shouted. "I am innocent! Let me go!" But no one listened. No one came.
Days became months. Months became years. Edmond was cold, hungry, and alone. He almost went mad. He almost gave up hope. Sometimes he wanted to die.
He did not know that outside, his life was being stolen.

His enemy Fernand married Mercédès, who believed Edmond was gone forever. Danglars became rich and powerful. Villefort became an important, respected judge. The bad men were winning. The good man was rotting in a prison cell.
Edmond spent fourteen years in that cell. Fourteen years for a crime he did not do.
But one day, everything changed.
Chapter 5. The Old Priest.
One night, Edmond heard a strange sound. It came from behind the wall of his cell. Someone was digging.
For many days, Edmond dug too, from his side. At last, a hole opened in the wall. An old man came through it.
The old man was a priest named Abbé Faria. He was also a prisoner. For years, he had been digging a tunnel to escape, but the tunnel had led to Edmond's cell instead of to freedom.

The two men became close friends. Faria was very wise and clever. He had many books in his mind. Every day, he taught Edmond — languages, history, science, and much more. The young sailor became an educated, brilliant man.
One day, Faria asked Edmond about his story. Edmond told him everything: the ship, the wedding, the arrest.
Faria listened carefully. He was clever, and he understood things Edmond could not see.
"My poor friend," Faria said. "Do you not understand? You were not arrested by mistake. Three men did this to you. They were jealous. They planned it all."
And Faria helped Edmond see the truth: the names of the men who had destroyed his life — Danglars, Fernand, and Villefort.
Edmond's sadness turned into something hard and cold. He wanted revenge.
Chapter 6. The Secret Treasure.
Old Faria was growing weak and ill. He knew he did not have long to live.
One day, he called Edmond close and told him a great secret.

"I know where there is a treasure," Faria whispered. "A huge treasure, hidden long ago on a small island. The island is called Monte Cristo. No one else knows about it. Gold, jewels, riches beyond your dreams. If you ever escape, go there. The treasure is yours."
Edmond did not know if he could believe such a story. But Faria gave him careful directions and made him remember every detail.
Not long after, Abbé Faria became very sick, and he died.
Edmond was heartbroken. His only friend was gone. But Faria had given him two gifts: knowledge, and the secret of the treasure.
And now, looking at his dead friend, Edmond had a bold and dangerous idea for how to escape.
Chapter 7. The Escape.
When a prisoner died in the Château d'If, the guards put the body in a strong bag. Then they carried it out and threw it into the deep sea.
Edmond made his plan quickly. He moved his dead friend's body into his own cell and put it in his own bed. Then Edmond climbed inside the body bag himself, in the dead man's place.
That night, the guards came. They did not look closely. They picked up the bag with Edmond inside it. They carried it to the edge of the high prison wall.
"One, two, three!" they said. And they threw the bag into the sea.
Edmond fell down, down, into the cold, dark water. Quickly, he cut open the bag with a small knife he had hidden. He swam up to the surface and took a deep breath of fresh air.
He was free! After fourteen years, Edmond Dantès was free.
He swam through the dark water until a passing boat found him and pulled him out. He was alive, and the whole world thought he was dead. That was exactly what he needed.
Chapter 8. The Count Is Born.
Edmond found a way to travel to the small island of Monte Cristo.
He searched for the hidden treasure, following old Faria's directions. He dug and looked. And then he found it — a secret cave, full of gold and jewels.
Faria's story was true. Edmond was now one of the richest men in the world.
But Edmond Dantès, the young sailor, was gone forever. In his place stood a new man: cold, powerful, mysterious, and very rich. He gave himself a grand new name.
He became the Count of Monte Cristo.
No one knew his true face. His enemies thought Edmond Dantès was dead. So the Count could walk right up to them, smile at them, and they would never know who he really was.
He had two plans. He would reward the people who had been good to him. And he would punish the people who had destroyed his life.
Slowly, patiently, he began.
Chapter 9. Rewarding the Good.
First, the Count remembered the good.

Monsieur Morrel, the kind ship owner, had always believed in Edmond and had tried to help him. Now, years later, Morrel was old and in trouble. His business was failing. He was about to lose everything.
The Count of Monte Cristo secretly saved him. He paid Morrel's debts and gave his family hope again, all without saying who he really was.
Morrel and his family cried with joy and thanked the mysterious stranger who had saved them. They never knew it was the young sailor they had once helped.
The Count felt happy for a moment. Kindness was returned with kindness.
But he had not forgotten the others. Now it was time for revenge.
Chapter 10. Revenge.

One by one, the Count found his three enemies. They were now rich and powerful men in the city of Paris. They did not know that the polite, mysterious Count was really the man they had sent to prison.

The Count was patient and clever. He did not simply attack them. Instead, he learned all their secrets. Each of the three men had done other bad things over the years. The Count slowly brought those secrets into the light.
Danglars, who loved money most of all, lost all of his money and was ruined.

Fernand, who had stolen Mercédès, was shown to be a liar and a traitor. His secrets were revealed to everyone. He lost his good name, his family, and his honour, and in his shame, he ended his own life.
Villefort, the judge who had hidden the truth, had dark secrets in his own family. When they all came out, his life fell apart, and his mind broke.
One by one, the men who had destroyed Edmond Dantès were destroyed themselves. Justice, cold and complete, had come at last.
Chapter 11. Wait and Hope.
The Count of Monte Cristo had won. His enemies were punished. But revenge did not feel as sweet as he had imagined.

Along the way, innocent people had been hurt too, and the Count felt the weight of that. He saw Mercédès again, old and sad now, and he understood that the happy young man he once was could never come back. The past was gone. Some things could not be fixed.
The Count began to feel that pure revenge was not the answer to everything. He learned that only God can be a perfect judge. He decided to stop, and to leave the past behind.

He gave gifts of money and happiness to the young people he cared about. And there was a kind and beautiful young woman named Haydée, whom he had saved from a terrible life. She loved him truly. And slowly, the Count found that he loved her too.
Together, they sailed away across the sea to start a new life, far from all the pain.
Before he left, the Count sent a message to his young friends, words to remember for the rest of their lives:
"All human wisdom is contained in these two words — wait and hope."

Edmond Dantès had waited in the dark for fourteen years. He had never fully lost hope. And in the end, after all the sadness and all the revenge, he sailed toward a new life and a new love, free at last.
The End.
Chapter 1. Call Me Ishmael.
Call me Ishmael.
I was a young man with no money and no plan. I felt sad and tired of life on land. When I feel this way, I know what to do. I go to sea.
So I decided to join a whaling ship. On a whaling ship, men sail across the ocean to hunt whales — the biggest animals in the world. It is hard, dangerous work. But I wanted adventure.
I travelled to a town by the sea. It was cold and dark. I needed a bed for the night, but the inn was full. The innkeeper said I would have to share a room, and a bed, with another man — a harpooner.
"A harpooner?" I said. A harpooner throws the long spear that kills the whale.
"Yes," said the innkeeper. "But be careful. He is a strange one."
I did not like the sound of this. But I was tired, so I agreed.
Chapter 2. Queequeg.
Late that night, the harpooner came into the room.

He was a big man from a faraway island in the South Seas. His skin was covered with dark tattoos, all over his body and face. He carried a sharp harpoon. At first, I was very afraid of him. I thought he might be dangerous.
His name was Queequeg.
But I was wrong to be afraid. Queequeg was kind and honest. He had a good, brave heart. We talked, and soon we were friends. In fact, we became best friends. Queequeg said we were like brothers now.
"We go to sea together," Queequeg said. "You and me. Good friends."
I was happy. In this cold, lonely world, I had found a true friend.
The next day, Queequeg and I went to find a ship.
Chapter 3. The Ship Pequod.
We found a whaling ship called the Pequod. It was an old ship, strong and a little frightening to look at. It had sailed the seas for many years.
Queequeg was a famous harpooner, so the ship's owners were happy to take him. And they took me too, as a simple sailor.
I asked about the captain of the ship. His name was Captain Ahab.
"Where is the captain?" I asked. "I would like to meet him."
"Captain Ahab is not here yet," a sailor said. "He stays in his room. You will see him when we are at sea. He is... a special man. He had a hard time on his last voyage."
This was strange. But I did not think much about it. I was excited to sail. Soon, the Pequod left the land behind. We sailed out into the wide, open ocean.
For many days, we did not see the captain at all.
Chapter 4. Captain Ahab.
Then, one morning, Captain Ahab came up onto the deck.
I will never forget the first time I saw him. He was tall and old, with a hard, serious face. There was a long white scar down his skin. But the strangest thing was his leg.
One of his legs was gone. In its place, he had a leg made of white whale bone — smooth and pale, like ivory. When he walked, it made a hard tapping sound on the wooden deck. Tap, tap, tap.
Captain Ahab stood strong and proud, even with his bone leg. But his eyes were dark and sad and angry, all at the same time. There was a storm inside this man.
"What happened to his leg?" I asked another sailor quietly.
The sailor looked around to make sure no one was listening.
"A whale," he whispered. "A great white whale. It bit off the captain's leg. A famous whale, known by all the sailors. Its name is Moby Dick."
Chapter 5. The Gold Coin.
A few days later, Captain Ahab called all the sailors to the deck.
He held up a shining gold coin. It was worth a lot of money.
"Look at this gold!" Ahab shouted. "I will give it to the first man who sees a certain whale. A great white whale, with a wrinkled head. A whale called Moby Dick!"
The sailors were excited about the gold.
Then Ahab nailed the coin to the tall wooden mast in the middle of the ship, so everyone could see it every day.

"Listen to me!" Ahab cried, his eyes burning. "This white whale took my leg. This is why we are really here. Not just for money. Not just for other whales. We are here to find Moby Dick — and to kill him! We will chase him around the whole world if we must!"
The sailors shouted and cheered. Ahab's anger filled them all.
Only one man did not cheer.
Chapter 6. Starbuck's Warning.
The first mate — the captain's most important helper — was a good, careful man named Starbuck.
Starbuck did not like Ahab's plan. He came to the captain quietly.

"Captain," Starbuck said, "we are here to hunt whales for their oil, to make money for the ship's owners. That is our job. But to chase one whale, for revenge? That is madness. It is only a dumb animal. It did not hate you. It only acted like a whale. Why risk all our lives for revenge?"
Ahab's face grew dark.
"You do not understand," Ahab said. "This is not about a whale. It is about the evil in the world. I will fight it. I will not stop. Not for anything. Not for anyone."
Starbuck saw that he could not change the captain's mind. Ahab's need for revenge was too strong. It had become the only thing he cared about.
Starbuck walked away, full of fear. He looked at the wide sea and felt that something terrible was coming.
Chapter 7. The Long Hunt.
The Pequod sailed on and on, across many seas.

Sometimes we saw other whales, and we hunted them. The sailors got into small boats and rowed close to the great animals. Queequeg threw his harpoon. It was dangerous and exciting. Whales are huge and strong, and men can die in this work.
Sometimes we met other whaling ships on the sea. Captain Ahab always asked them the same question, shouting across the water:
"Have you seen the white whale? Have you seen Moby Dick?"
Some ships said no. But some said yes. And one captain had a warning.
"We saw the white whale," this captain said. "Do not chase him! He is too strong. He destroyed our boats. He hurt my men. Turn away, friend, while you can!"
But Ahab did not listen. The news that Moby Dick was near only made his eyes shine brighter.
"Which way?" Ahab shouted. "Which way did he go?"
We were getting closer. Everyone could feel it. The whole ship was tense and quiet.
Chapter 8. The White Whale.
Then, one clear day, Captain Ahab himself saw it first.

Far across the water, something huge and white rose up. It was a whale bigger than any I had ever seen. Its skin was pale, almost white, and its head was wrinkled and old. It moved through the water slowly, calmly, like a king of the sea.
Moby Dick.
"There he blows!" Ahab screamed with wild joy. "The white whale! Now we have him! Lower the boats!"
The sailors were both excited and afraid. This was the moment. This was the reason for the whole long journey.
The men climbed into the small boats and began to row toward the giant white whale. Ahab led them, standing in the front of his boat, his bone leg firm, his harpoon ready.
The great chase began.
Chapter 9. The Battle.
For three days, we chased the white whale.

On the first day, the boats came close. But Moby Dick was too strong. He turned and smashed the boats to pieces with his huge body. The men fell into the water. We saved them, but the whale swam away.
On the second day, we chased him again. Again the whale fought back. He broke more boats. Good men were hurt. Even now, Ahab would not stop.
"Tomorrow," Ahab said, breathing hard. "Tomorrow we will kill him."
Starbuck begged him one last time. "Captain, please! Two days of this! Look at the men we have lost! Let us turn back. This is not too late. Please!"
But Ahab's heart was closed. "It is my fate," he said quietly. "I cannot turn away now. I was born for this."
On the third day, we found Moby Dick again. And the final battle began.
Chapter 10. The End.
On the third day, Ahab threw his harpoon with all his strength. It struck the white whale.

But the whale was too powerful. In pain and anger, Moby Dick turned and attacked the ship itself — the great Pequod. He hit it again and again with his enormous head. Water rushed in. The ship began to sink.

Ahab, in his small boat, threw his harpoon one last time. The sharp rope flew out. But it caught around Ahab's own neck. As the whale dived down into the deep sea, it pulled Ahab with it, down into the dark water. He was gone in a moment, still holding on to his enemy at the very end.

The great white whale swam away and disappeared. And the Pequod sank beneath the waves. All the boats were destroyed. The sailors were lost in the sea. Brave Queequeg, kind Starbuck, mad Captain Ahab — all of them gone.
All except one.
Me. Ishmael.

When the ship went down, a wooden coffin floated up to the top of the water. It was empty, and it kept me from sinking. I held on to it for a whole day and a night, alone in the middle of the huge, quiet ocean.
At last, another ship found me and pulled me from the water. I was the only man saved. I lived to tell this story.

Captain Ahab had wanted revenge more than anything else in the world. In the end, his revenge cost him his ship, his crew, and his life. He chased the great white whale to the ends of the earth — and the great white whale took everything from him.
And the sea, as always, rolled on, deep and calm, as if none of it had ever happened.
The End.
Chapter 1. The Hero Who Wanted to Go Home.
Long, long ago, there was a great war. It was called the Trojan War. Many Greek heroes fought in it. One of the cleverest was a man named Odysseus.
Odysseus was brave and very smart. He always had a good plan. After ten long years, the war ended, and the Greeks won. Now the heroes could go home.

But for Odysseus, going home was not easy. His home was a small island called Ithaca. There, his wife Penelope and his young son Telemachus were waiting for him. Odysseus loved them very much. All he wanted was to see them again.
But the sea was full of danger. And one of the gods, the sea god Poseidon, would become his enemy. Odysseus did not know it yet, but his journey home would take another ten years.

At home in Ithaca, things were bad. Everyone thought Odysseus was dead. Many rude, greedy men came to his house. They wanted to marry Penelope and take Odysseus's kingdom. They ate his food and drank his wine and would not leave. Penelope did not want any of them. She still hoped her husband would come home. But she was afraid, and she was almost out of hope.
Chapter 2. The One-Eyed Giant.
On his way home, Odysseus and his men landed on a strange island. They were hungry, so they went to look for food.
They found a big cave full of cheese and animals. They went inside to eat. But the cave belonged to a monster.
The monster was a Cyclops — a giant as big as a mountain, with only one huge eye in the middle of his head. His name was Polyphemus.
The Cyclops came home with his sheep. He rolled a giant stone across the door of the cave, so no one could get out. Then he saw the men.
"Who are you?" he shouted.
Before Odysseus could speak, the giant grabbed two of his men and ate them. The other men screamed in fear. They were trapped. The stone was too heavy to move. They could not escape.
Odysseus had to think of a clever plan, and think fast.
Chapter 3. The Clever Trick.
Odysseus had an idea.
He gave the giant strong wine to drink. The Cyclops loved it. "Give me more!" he said. He drank and drank.
"What is your name?" the giant asked.
"My name," said Odysseus with a smile, "is Nobody."
"Well, Nobody," said the giant, laughing, "I will eat you last. That is my gift to you." Then the Cyclops fell into a deep sleep from all the wine.
Now Odysseus acted. He and his men took a long, sharp wooden pole. They pushed it into the giant's one big eye. The Cyclops woke up screaming in pain. Now he was blind!
Other giants heard him shouting. "Polyphemus! What is wrong? Is someone hurting you?" they called.
"Nobody is hurting me!" the giant screamed.
"Nobody?" said the other giants. "Then be quiet and go to sleep!" And they went away. Odysseus's trick had worked.

In the morning, the blind giant opened the door to let his sheep out. He felt each sheep to make sure no men were escaping. But Odysseus and his men were hiding under the sheep, holding on to their thick wool. So they escaped from the cave!
Chapter 4. The Angry God.
Odysseus and his men ran to their ship and sailed away fast.
But Odysseus was too proud. He called back to the giant across the water.
"Cyclops! If anyone asks who blinded you, tell them it was Odysseus!"
This was a big mistake. Because the Cyclops was the son of Poseidon, the god of the sea.

The blind giant lifted his hands and prayed to his father. "Father Poseidon! A man named Odysseus has hurt me. Punish him! Do not let him reach his home. And if he does get home, let it be after many years, alone, with all his men dead!"
Poseidon heard his son. From that day, the sea god was angry with Odysseus. He sent storms and waves and danger. He made the journey long and hard.
Odysseus did not know it, but he had just made a powerful enemy.
Chapter 5. The Witch.
The journey went on. Odysseus and his men landed on another island. On this island lived a beautiful witch named Circe.
Circe invited some of the men into her house. She gave them a lovely meal. But the food had magic in it. As soon as the men ate, they changed into pigs! Circe laughed and pushed them into a pen.
When Odysseus heard this, he went to save his men. A friendly god gave him a special plant to protect him from the magic. So when Circe tried her magic on Odysseus, it did not work.
Odysseus took out his sword. "Change my men back!" he said. "Now!"
Circe was surprised. No one had ever escaped her magic before. She saw that Odysseus was special. She changed the pigs back into men, and after that she was kind to them.
Odysseus and his men stayed on the island and rested for a while. But Odysseus never forgot his true home. Soon it was time to sail again.
Chapter 6. The Song and the Monster.
The next part of the journey was full of danger.
First, they had to pass the Sirens. The Sirens were creatures who sang the most beautiful songs in the world. But the songs were a trap. Any sailor who heard them jumped into the sea and died.

Odysseus wanted to hear the beautiful song and live. So he made a plan. He put soft wax in his men's ears, so they could not hear anything. Then he told them to tie him tightly to the ship, so he could not move.
As they passed, Odysseus heard the beautiful, deadly song. He wanted to jump. He shouted and pulled at the ropes. But his men could not hear him, and they did not untie him. So they passed safely.

Then they had to sail through a narrow sea. On one side was a terrible six-headed monster. On the other side was a giant whirlpool that could swallow the whole ship. Odysseus steered close to the monster. It grabbed and ate six of his men. It was terrible. But the rest of the ship got through.
Odysseus was losing his men, one by one. But he kept sailing toward home.
Chapter 7. The Last of the Men.
Tired and hungry, the men landed on another island. On this island lived cattle — but they were not ordinary cattle. They belonged to the great Sun god.
"Do not touch these animals," Odysseus warned his men. "They are holy. If we hurt them, the gods will punish us."
But bad weather trapped them on the island for a long time. Their food ran out. The men were starving. So, while Odysseus was sleeping, they killed some of the Sun god's cattle and ate them.
The Sun god was furious. He asked the great god Zeus to punish the men.
When they sailed away, Zeus sent a huge storm. Lightning struck the ship, and it broke apart. All of Odysseus's men drowned in the sea.
Only Odysseus was saved. He held on to a piece of broken wood and floated alone on the wide ocean. He had lost his ship. He had lost every one of his men. Now he was truly alone.
Chapter 8. Alone, and Then Free.
Odysseus floated to an island where a beautiful goddess named Calypso lived.
Calypso liked Odysseus and wanted him to stay with her forever. She kept him on her island for many years. Her island was lovely, but it was not his home.

Every day, Odysseus sat by the sea and looked toward Ithaca. He missed his wife. He missed his son. He cried for his home. No beautiful island could make him happy, because it was not the place he loved.
At last, the gods felt pity for Odysseus. The goddess Athena had always liked Odysseus, because he was clever and brave. She spoke to the other gods. "It is time," she said. "Let him go home."

So the gods ordered Calypso to set Odysseus free. She helped him build a small boat, and he sailed away at last. Poseidon sent one more terrible storm, but with the gods' help, Odysseus finally reached the shore of his own island, Ithaca.
After twenty years, Odysseus was home. But his troubles were not over yet.
Chapter 9. The Beggar.
Odysseus could not just walk into his house. The greedy men were still there, eating his food and bothering his wife. There were many of them, and only one of him.
So the goddess Athena helped him with a clever disguise. She made Odysseus look like a poor old beggar in dirty clothes. No one knew it was really the great hero.
In secret, Odysseus found his son, Telemachus, who was now a young man. Odysseus showed his son his true face. They hugged, full of joy and tears. Together, they made a plan to defeat the greedy men.
Dressed as a beggar, Odysseus went into his own house. The rude men laughed at him and were cruel to him. Odysseus said nothing. He waited. He watched. He was patient.
His wife Penelope did not know the beggar was really her husband. But she was tired of the greedy men. So she made an announcement.
"I will hold a contest," Penelope said. "Here is my husband's great bow. Whoever can use this bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axe-heads — I will marry that man."
Chapter 10. The Return of the King.
The contest began.
One by one, the greedy men tried to use the great bow. But it was too strong for them. Not one of them could even bend it. They pushed and pulled, but they failed.
Then the old beggar spoke. "Let me try," he said.
The men laughed. "A dirty old beggar? Try, then. It is funny to watch."
Odysseus picked up the bow. And easily, quietly, he bent it and pulled the string. Then he shot the arrow straight through all twelve axe-heads.
The room went silent. How could a beggar do this?
Then Odysseus threw off his rags. "I am Odysseus!" he shouted. "I have come home!"

The greedy men were filled with fear. Odysseus and his son Telemachus fought them. Odysseus was the greatest fighter of his age, and Athena helped him. One by one, the men who had eaten his food and troubled his wife were defeated. At last, his house was clear.
Then came the most important moment. Odysseus stood before Penelope. She looked at him for a long time. She was careful. After twenty years, could this really be her husband?
She tested him with a secret that only the real Odysseus would know, about how their bed was made. When Odysseus answered correctly, Penelope's heart filled with joy. It was truly him.
They ran into each other's arms and cried with happiness. After twenty years of war, monsters, storms, and loss, Odysseus was home at last, with the wife and son he loved.
His long, hard journey was finally over. And they lived, together, in peace.
The End.
Chapter 1. The Great War.
Long ago, there was a great city called Troy. It had high, strong walls.
For nine years, a huge army from Greece had camped outside the city. The Greeks wanted to break into Troy and win the war. But the walls were too strong, and the people of Troy fought back bravely.

Why was there a war? Because of a woman named Helen. Helen was the most beautiful woman in the world. She was the wife of a Greek king. But a prince of Troy named Paris took her away to Troy. The Greeks were angry, so they sailed to Troy to get her back. And so the long war began.
The greatest fighter among the Greeks was a man named Achilles. He was strong, fast, and almost impossible to beat in battle. When Achilles fought, the enemy ran away in fear.
The greatest fighter among the people of Troy was a prince named Hector. Hector was brave and good. He loved his city, his father, his wife, and his little son. He fought to protect his home.
These two great men would meet before the end. But first, there was trouble in the Greek camp.
Chapter 2. The Quarrel.
The leader of the Greek army was a proud king named Agamemnon.

Agamemnon and Achilles had an argument. It was about a prize — a young woman who had been taken in the war. Agamemnon had to give up his prize. So, to feel better, he took Achilles's prize instead. Her name was Briseis.
Achilles was furious. Agamemnon had shamed him in front of everyone.
"I am the best fighter in this whole army!" Achilles shouted. "I do all the hard fighting. And you, Agamemnon, you take my prize? You have no right!"
"I am the king," said Agamemnon coldly. "I do what I want. The girl is mine now."
Achilles was so angry that he almost drew his sword. But he stopped himself. Instead, he made a terrible decision.
"Fine," Achilles said. "Then I will not fight anymore. Let us see how you do without me. The Greeks will lose, and it will be your fault."
Chapter 3. Achilles Will Not Fight.
Achilles went back to his tent. He would not come out. He would not fight.
His soldiers stayed with him and rested. The greatest warrior in the world sat and did nothing, while the war went on without him.
Achilles was still full of anger and hurt pride. He wanted Agamemnon to feel sorry. He wanted the Greeks to see how much they needed him.
Day after day, he stayed away from the battle.
And slowly, his wish came true — but in a way that would bring him great pain.
Chapter 4. Losing the War.
Without Achilles, the Greeks began to lose.
Brave Hector led the people of Troy out of the city gates. He fought like a lion. He pushed the Greeks back, again and again.

The Trojans drove the Greeks all the way back to the sea, where the Greek ships were. Hector's men even began to set fire to the ships. If the ships burned, the Greeks could never go home. It was a disaster.
The Greek leaders were afraid. They went to Achilles and begged him.
"Please, Achilles," they said. "We are sorry. Agamemnon will give back your prize and much more. Just come back and fight! We are losing! We will all die!"
But Achilles was still too proud and too angry. "No," he said. "Let them lose. Let Agamemnon see what happens without me."
His heart was hard. He did not know that his anger would soon cost him the person he loved most.
Chapter 5. Patroclus.
Achilles had a very dear friend named Patroclus. They had grown up together. They loved each other like brothers.
Patroclus watched the Greeks dying, and his heart broke. He could not just sit and do nothing while his friends were killed.

"Achilles," Patroclus said, "if you will not fight, then let me fight. Let me wear your armour. When the Trojans see your armour, they will think you have returned. They will be afraid, and the Greeks will have hope again. Please. Let me help our friends."
Achilles thought about it. At last, he agreed.
"All right," Achilles said. "Wear my armour. Push the Trojans back from the ships. But be careful. Do not chase them all the way to the walls of Troy. Come back safe. Promise me."
"I promise," said Patroclus.
He put on Achilles's shining armour. He looked just like the great warrior himself. Then he led Achilles's soldiers into battle.
Chapter 6. The Death of Patroclus.
When the Trojans saw the famous armour, they were filled with fear. "Achilles is back!" they cried, and they began to run.
Patroclus fought bravely. He pushed the Trojans back, away from the ships. He saved the Greeks. He was a hero that day.
But Patroclus forgot Achilles's warning. Full of the excitement of battle, he chased the Trojans all the way to the walls of Troy.
There, Hector was waiting.
Hector and Patroclus fought. It was a hard fight. But Hector was one of the greatest warriors in the world. In the end, Hector struck Patroclus down.
As Patroclus lay dying, Hector took the shining armour of Achilles from his body.
The news travelled fast across the battlefield, back to Achilles's tent. His best friend was dead.
Chapter 7. Grief and Rage.
When Achilles heard that Patroclus was dead, he fell to the ground.
He cried out in pain. He put dirt on his head. He wept and wept. His grief was so great and so loud that people far away could hear it.
His anger at Agamemnon was gone now. It felt small and foolish. In its place was a new, burning feeling: rage against Hector, the man who had killed his friend.
"I will make Hector pay," Achilles said through his tears. "I will find him, and I will kill him. Nothing will stop me."
Now Achilles wanted to fight — not for Agamemnon, not for the war, but for Patroclus.
But he had a problem. His armour was gone. Hector had taken it. Achilles needed new armour before he could fight.
Chapter 8. The New Armour.
Achilles's mother was a goddess of the sea. She loved her son and saw his terrible grief.

She went to a god who could make wonderful things, and she asked him to make new armour for Achilles. The god worked all night and made the most beautiful armour ever seen. The shield was covered with pictures, and everything shone like fire.
When Achilles put on the new armour, he looked like a god of war. His face was terrible to see, full of grief and anger.
He walked out toward the battlefield. The very sight of him made the Trojans afraid. They knew that the greatest fighter in the world had returned, and that he was hungry for revenge.
Achilles attacked. He was like a storm. He drove the Trojans back toward their city, killing many along the way. The Trojans ran through their gates to safety.
All except one.
Chapter 9. Achilles and Hector.
Only Hector stayed outside the walls of Troy.
His father and mother stood on the wall and begged him. "Hector! Come inside! Do not fight Achilles! He is too strong! You will die!"
Hector was afraid. But he was also a man of honour. He felt it was his duty to fight. So he waited outside the gates for Achilles.
But when Achilles came close, full of rage, even brave Hector felt fear. He turned and ran. Achilles chased him around the walls of the city, three times around.
At last, Hector stopped and turned to face Achilles. He knew he could not run forever.
"Let us fight," Hector said. "And let us make one promise. If I win, I will treat your body with respect. If you win, promise to do the same for me."
"No," said Achilles coldly. His heart was full of grief for Patroclus. "There are no promises between us."
They fought. And Achilles, the greatest warrior of all, struck Hector down. The brave prince of Troy was dead.

But Achilles's grief made him cruel. He tied Hector's body to his chariot and dragged it in the dust, round and round, in front of the walls of Troy. On the wall, Hector's father and mother watched and cried. It was a terrible, shameful thing to do.
Chapter 10. A Father's Tears.
Hector's father was the old king of Troy. His name was Priam. His heart was broken. His best son was dead, and his body was not even given a proper burial.
That night, old King Priam did a very brave thing. Alone, in secret, he left the safe walls of Troy. He went across the dark battlefield, right into the enemy camp, to the tent of Achilles.
The old king knelt down before the man who had killed his son. He took Achilles's hands — the same hands that had killed Hector — and he kissed them.

"Great Achilles," Priam said, with tears in his eyes. "Think of your own father. He is old, like me. Please, have pity on an old man. Give me back the body of my son, so I can bury him. That is all I ask."

Achilles looked at the crying old man. And suddenly, his anger melted away. He thought of his own father, far away. He thought of Patroclus. He thought of how much sadness this war had brought to everyone.
Achilles began to cry too. The two men, enemies, wept together — one for a dead son, one for a dead friend.
"Yes," Achilles said gently. "You may take your son home. I am sorry for your pain."
Achilles gave Hector's body back to his father, with respect. He even agreed to stop the fighting for a while, so the people of Troy could bury their prince.
So Hector, the brave prince, was carried home. The people of Troy cried for him and gave him a great funeral.

The war was not over. Troy would fall in the end, and many more would die. But in that quiet moment between two crying men — one Greek, one Trojan — something more important than war appeared. It was pity. It was understanding. It was the reminder that even enemies are human, and that all men know grief.
The End.
Chapter 1. The Young Man from the Country.
Long ago in France, there lived a brave young man named d'Artagnan. He was seventeen years old. He came from a small country town, and he was poor. But he had a big dream.
d'Artagnan wanted to be a Musketeer.
The Musketeers were the special soldiers of the King of France. They were the best fighters in the country. They were brave and famous, and they carried swords. Everyone admired them.
So d'Artagnan said goodbye to his family. He got on his horse and rode all the way to the big city of Paris. He had almost no money, only his sword and his courage.
"One day," he said to himself, "I will be a great Musketeer. I will serve the King. People will know my name!"
He did not know that his adventures would begin the very moment he arrived.
Chapter 2. Three New Friends.
On his first day in Paris, d'Artagnan had a bad start. He was young and quick to anger. By accident, he made three different men angry with him. Each one challenged him to a sword fight.
But these three men were not just anyone. They were three of the most famous Musketeers in Paris.
The first was Athos. He was serious, quiet, and noble. He seemed to carry a secret sadness.
The second was Porthos. He was big, strong, and loud. He loved fine clothes and good food.
The third was Aramis. He was gentle and clever, and one day he wanted to become a priest.

d'Artagnan was ready to fight all three of them, one after another. But before the fights could begin, something happened. The guards of the Cardinal — the King's rival — appeared. The Cardinal's guards were the enemies of the Musketeers.
Suddenly, d'Artagnan and the three Musketeers were on the same side. They drew their swords and fought the Cardinal's guards together. And they won!
Chapter 3. All for One.
After the fight, the three Musketeers looked at d'Artagnan with new respect.
"You fight very well, young man," said Athos. "You are brave. You fought beside us like a true Musketeer."
d'Artagnan was proud and happy. He was not an official Musketeer yet, but now he had three powerful friends.
The four men became close. They went everywhere together. They shared their money, their food, and their adventures. They trusted each other completely.
And they had a special promise, a motto they lived by:
"All for one, and one for all!"

It meant that they would always help each other. If one of them was in danger, the others would come. If one of them was in trouble, they all shared it. Their friendship was the most important thing in their lives.
Soon, this friendship would be tested by a dangerous secret.
Chapter 4. The Queen's Secret.
In France, there was a King and a beautiful Queen. But the King and Queen were not happy together.

The most powerful man in France, after the King, was the Cardinal. The Cardinal was clever and cold. He had spies everywhere. And he did not like the Queen. He wanted to find a way to shame her in front of the King.

The Queen had a secret. As a gift, the King had once given her a beautiful set of twelve diamonds. But the Queen had secretly given those diamonds to a good friend of hers, a nobleman from England called the Duke of Buckingham.
The Cardinal learned this secret. And he made an evil plan.
The Cardinal told the King, "You should have a great ball. And you should ask the Queen to wear her beautiful diamonds."
The King thought this was a fine idea. He told the Queen to wear the diamonds to the ball, in just a few days.
The Queen was terrified. The diamonds were in England! If she could not wear them, the King would know she had given them away. She would be shamed and ruined.
Chapter 5. A Dangerous Job.
The Queen needed help. Secretly, she asked a kind young woman named Constance to help her. And Constance knew exactly who to ask.
Constance went to d'Artagnan. And d'Artagnan had already fallen in love with her.

"d'Artagnan," Constance said, "the Queen is in great danger. She needs someone brave to travel to England and bring the diamonds back — before the ball. But the journey is dangerous. The Cardinal's men will try to stop you. Will you help?"
"I will do it," said d'Artagnan at once. "For the Queen. And for you."
But he knew he could not do it alone. So he went to his three friends.
"My friends," he said, "I have a dangerous job. It is for the Queen of France. We may be hurt. We may even die. Will you come with me?"
The three Musketeers did not even ask what the job was.
"All for one, and one for all!" they said. "We will come."
Chapter 6. The Race to England.
The four friends got on their horses and rode fast toward the coast, to catch a boat to England.
But the Cardinal's spies were watching. Along the road, again and again, the Cardinal's men tried to stop them.

At one place, Porthos stayed behind to fight the enemy, so the others could go on. At another place, Aramis was stopped. Then Athos, too, had to stay and fight. One by one, the brave Musketeers fell behind, each one fighting to protect the others.
In the end, only d'Artagnan was left. He rode on alone, faster and faster. His friends had given everything so that he could keep going. He could not let them down.
"All for one," he whispered as he rode. "I must not stop."
At last, tired and hurt, d'Artagnan reached the sea. He got on a boat and crossed the water to England.
Chapter 7. The Diamonds.
In England, d'Artagnan found the Duke of Buckingham.
"Your Grace," said d'Artagnan, "the Queen is in danger. She needs her diamonds back at once, or she will be ruined."
The Duke went to get the diamonds. But when he looked at them, he found something terrible.
Two of the twelve diamonds were missing!
Someone had stolen them. That someone was a beautiful, dangerous woman named Milady — a secret spy who worked for the Cardinal. She had cut two diamonds from the set to help ruin the Queen.
But the Duke did not give up. He called for the best jewel-makers in England and paid them a lot of money.
"Work all night," he told them. "Make two new diamonds, exactly the same as the others. No one must see any difference."
The jewel-makers worked very hard and very fast. By morning, the two new diamonds were ready. Now there were twelve again, and they looked perfect.
d'Artagnan took the diamonds, thanked the Duke, and raced back toward France. But time was running out. The ball was almost here.
Chapter 8. Saving the Queen.
d'Artagnan rode like the wind. He crossed the sea and rushed back through France, day and night, without stopping to rest.
He arrived in Paris just in time.

At the palace, the great ball had begun. The King was there, dressed in gold. The Cardinal was there too, smiling his cold smile. He was sure that the Queen had no diamonds, and that she would be shamed at last.
The King turned to the Queen. "My dear," he said, "where are your diamonds? Why are you not wearing them?"
The Cardinal watched, waiting for his victory.
But then the Queen smiled. She was wearing the diamonds! All twelve of them shone brightly on her dress. d'Artagnan had gotten them back to her just in time.
The King was pleased. And the Cardinal was shocked and angry. His evil plan had failed. He did not know how, but somehow the Queen had been saved.
The Queen looked across the room and gave a tiny, secret smile of thanks to d'Artagnan. He had saved her honour. He was a hero.
Chapter 9. The Dangerous Woman.
But the story was not over. The Cardinal's spy, Milady, was very angry that her plan had failed. And she blamed d'Artagnan.
Milady was the most dangerous enemy of all. She was beautiful, but her heart was cold and cruel. She had done many evil things in her life. She would stop at nothing to get revenge.

Milady tried to hurt d'Artagnan again and again. And then she did something truly terrible. She poisoned sweet Constance, the woman d'Artagnan loved. Constance died, and d'Artagnan's heart was broken.
The three Musketeers saw how much pain Milady had caused. This cruel woman had hurt their friend, and she had done evil to many other people too. They decided that she had to be stopped for good.

Together, the four friends followed Milady and finally caught her. They put her on trial for all her crimes. And Milady, the dangerous spy, was punished for the terrible things she had done. At last, she could hurt no one else.
Chapter 10. The Reward.
The Cardinal was still the most powerful man in France. He knew that d'Artagnan and the Musketeers had beaten his plans again and again.

A weaker man might have punished them. But the Cardinal was clever. He could see that d'Artagnan was brave, loyal, and skilled. And the Cardinal thought it was better to have such a young man as a friend than as an enemy.
So the Cardinal did something surprising. He gave d'Artagnan a great honour: a paper that made him an officer — a lieutenant in the Musketeers.

d'Artagnan's dream had come true. He had come to Paris as a poor country boy with nothing but a sword and his courage. Now he was a real Musketeer, and an officer too. He had served the King and Queen. He had gone on great adventures. And best of all, he had found three true friends who would stay with him for life.
Athos, Porthos, and Aramis stood beside him, proud and happy.
"All for one," they said together, "and one for all!"
And so the four friends went on to many more adventures, brave and loyal, always together, always ready to help each other, until the very end.
The End.
Chapter 1. A Room Like a Box.
It was a hot summer in the city of St. Petersburg. The streets smelled bad. The air was thick and heavy. A young man walked slowly along the road, with his head down.

His name was Rodion Raskolnikov. He was tall and thin. He had dark hair and dark eyes. His clothes were old and dirty, and his shoes were broken. But his face was clever. Not long ago, he was a university student. Now he had no money, and he had stopped his studies.

Rodion lived at the top of an old house, in a very small room. The room was like a box. The walls were yellow. The ceiling was so low that he could almost touch it with his hand. He owed money to the woman who owned the house, so now he was afraid of her. When he went down the stairs, he walked quietly, like a thief, so she would not see him.
He was hungry. He was hungry almost every day. But he did not think much about food. Something darker filled his mind.
For weeks, a terrible idea had lived inside his head. It grew bigger every day. It frightened him, but he could not stop thinking about it.

Near his house lived an old woman called Alyona Ivanovna. She lent money to poor people. If you gave her a watch or a ring, she gave you a little money. Then you had to pay her back much more. She was rich, but she was cruel. She lived with her younger sister, Lizaveta, a tall, quiet, gentle woman who worked like a servant and never said an unkind word.
Rodion had visited the old woman once, to sell a ring. He hated her. He thought she was like a small, ugly insect, useful to no one.

And this was his terrible idea: What if he killed her? She was old and cruel and useless. With her money, he could finish his studies. He could help his mother and his sister. He could do great things for the world.

He had a strange theory. He believed that most people must obey the law. But a few special people — great people, like kings and heroes — had the right to break the law, if it helped the world. These extraordinary people could even kill, and it was not really a crime.
"Am I one of those special people?" he asked himself. "Or am I weak, like everyone else?"
He wanted to know the answer. And he was afraid of it.
Chapter 2. The Plan.
One day, Rodion went to a small bar. There he met a sad man called Marmeladov. Marmeladov drank too much. He had lost his job. His family was poor and hungry.

"I have a daughter," Marmeladov told him, with tears in his eyes. "Her name is Sonya. She is a good, kind girl. But we had no money, no food. So Sonya sold herself on the streets to feed us. She gave us the money and said nothing. My sweet Sonya."

Rodion listened. He felt pity for this broken family. He walked Marmeladov home and saw the tiny, dirty room where they lived. He saw the hungry children and the tired, angry wife. Before he left, he put his last few coins on the window. Then he went out into the street and felt foolish, because now he had nothing.
That night he could not sleep. His idea was stronger than ever.
The next day, he learned something by chance. He heard that Lizaveta, the old woman's gentle sister, would be away from home the next evening at seven o'clock. So the old woman would be alone.
Rodion's heart beat fast. It felt like a sign. It felt like the moment was choosing him.

He found an old axe in the kitchen downstairs. He hid it inside his coat, under his arm. He took a small object wrapped in paper — a fake "gift" to sell to the old woman, to make her turn her back to him.
Then he walked to her house. Every step felt heavy. His hands were cold, even in the summer heat. A voice inside him said, "Stop. Go home." But his legs kept walking.
Chapter 3. The Crime.
Rodion climbed the dark stairs to the old woman's door. He knocked.
The door opened a little. Alyona Ivanovna looked out with her small, sharp eyes.
"I have something to sell," Rodion said quietly.
She let him in. The room was small and full of old things. She took the paper package from his hands and turned to look at it near the window.
For one second, her back was to him.
Rodion took the axe from under his coat. He lifted it. And he brought it down on her head.
She fell without a sound. It was done. His idea was now real, and it was horrible.
His hands shook. He took her keys and looked for the money. He found some and pushed it into his pockets. He felt sick. The room seemed to move around him.
Then he heard a small noise behind him.

He turned. Lizaveta was standing in the doorway. She had come home early. She saw her dead sister on the floor. She saw the axe in Rodion's hand. Her mouth opened, but she did not scream. She only lifted one arm, like a frightened child.
Rodion could not stop now. He struck her too.

Now there were two dead women in the room. Lizaveta had done nothing wrong. She was gentle and kind, and he had killed her. In that moment, Rodion understood something terrible: this was not the act of a great, special man. It was just murder.

He heard footsteps on the stairs. Someone was coming to visit the old woman. Rodion pushed the door shut and stood very still, hardly breathing, while men knocked and waited outside. At last they went away to find help. Rodion ran down the stairs, hid in an empty flat for a moment, then escaped into the street.
He put the axe back where he had found it. He returned to his little room, fell onto his bed, and lay there like a dead man.
Chapter 4. The Sickness.
After that night, Rodion was ill.
For days he lay in his room with a fever. He was hot, then cold. He talked in his sleep. He did not know if it was day or night. Sometimes he saw the two dead women in his dreams.
His friend Razumikhin found him. Razumikhin was a kind, strong, cheerful young man. He brought Rodion food and a doctor. He did not understand why his friend was so sick and so strange.
"You must eat," Razumikhin said. "You must get better."

But Rodion did not want help. He wanted to be alone. Every knock on the door made his heart jump. Every voice on the stairs filled him with fear. He was sure that everyone was looking at him. He was sure that his face showed the truth.

The whole city was talking about the murders. When Rodion heard people speak about them, he felt dizzy and had to hold the wall. Once, he even went back near the old woman's house, as if his feet needed to return to the place. He asked strange questions. He almost wanted to be caught.

His guilt was like a heavy stone inside his chest. He had believed his idea would make him free and strong. Instead, it had put a wall between him and every other person in the world. He could not tell anyone. He was completely alone with what he had done.

Money was in his pocket now, but he did not use it. He hid it under a stone in an empty yard and never went back for it. He had killed for money, and now he did not even want it. Nothing about his theory had come true.
Chapter 5. Sonya's Father.
One evening, Rodion was in the street when he saw a crowd. A man had been hit by a carriage and lay on the ground, badly hurt.
Rodion looked closer. It was Marmeladov, the sad man from the bar.
"I know him," Rodion said. "Take him to his home."
They carried Marmeladov to the small, poor room. His wife cried out. His children stood in the corner, pale and afraid. And then a young woman ran in.
It was Sonya. She was small and thin, with a soft, gentle face and frightened eyes. She knelt beside her dying father and held his hand.
Marmeladov looked at her. "Sonya," he whispered. "Forgive me." Then he died.
