Rodion watched Sonya. He saw her love, her sadness, her goodness. This girl had suffered so much, yet her heart was still kind and full of care. Something in Rodion moved. He took out the little money he had and gave it to the family for the funeral.
When he left, he felt strange — a small warm feeling in the cold darkness inside him. For a moment, helping this family made him feel human again.
He did not know it yet, but Sonya would become the most important person in his life.
Chapter 6. The Detective.
There was a clever detective in the city. His name was Porfiry Petrovich. It was his job to find the person who had killed the two women.
Porfiry was a calm man with a soft voice and small, smiling eyes. But behind his smile, his mind was sharp and quick. He watched people carefully. He listened to every word.

Porfiry had read something interesting: an article that Rodion had written months before, as a student. In the article, Rodion had explained his theory — that a few "extraordinary" people have the right to break the law for a great purpose.
Porfiry asked Rodion to come and talk. He was polite and friendly. He offered tea. But every question was like a small trap.
"Tell me about your article," Porfiry said gently. "This idea of yours — that some special men may kill. Very interesting. And tell me... do you think that you are one of these special men?"
Rodion felt cold. He tried to stay calm. "I only wrote about ideas," he said.
Porfiry smiled and nodded. He did not accuse Rodion. He did not have real proof. But he watched Rodion's face, his hands, his eyes. And Rodion understood: this quiet man suspected him.

It became a slow, silent game between them. Porfiry never shouted. He only smiled, asked questions, and waited. And with every meeting, the wall around Rodion's secret felt thinner. He knew that Porfiry was patient. He knew the detective was giving him time to break.
Chapter 7. Rodion and Sonya.
Rodion went to see Sonya.

Her room was strange and bare, in a poor house. She was surprised to see him, but she welcomed him kindly. They talked. Rodion looked at this gentle girl who did terrible work to save her family, and who still believed in God.
"How can you believe?" he asked her. "You have suffered so much. Your life is so hard."
"Without God, I would have nothing," Sonya said quietly. "I would have died long ago."

Rodion asked her to read to him from her old Bible. Her hands shook, but she read him the story of Lazarus — the story of a man who died and was brought back to life. As she read, her voice grew stronger. Rodion listened, and something in the story frightened and moved him. Could a dead man come back to life? Could a lost man be saved?

He came back to see her again and again. He did not fully understand why. Perhaps it was because Sonya was the only person who might understand suffering. Perhaps it was because he could not carry his secret alone any longer.
Sonya did not know his secret yet. But she felt his pain. She saw that he was carrying something heavy and dark. She looked at him with kind, worried eyes, and she wanted to help him.

Rodion's mother and his sister Dunya were in the city now too. They loved him and worried about him. But he pushed them away. He could not let them near him with such blood on his hands. His secret separated him from his own family, from everyone — everyone except Sonya.
Chapter 8. A Dangerous Man.

There was another man in the city called Svidrigailov. He was a cold, clever man with an empty smile. He had a dark past and few morals. He was interested in Rodion's sister, Dunya, and would not leave her alone.
By chance, Svidrigailov lived in the room next to Sonya's. And one day, through the thin wall, he heard something he was never meant to hear.
But that came a little later.

First, the pressure on Rodion grew and grew. Porfiry kept watching. The city kept talking. Rodion's fever came back. His guilt filled every hour of the day and every dream at night. He felt that he was going mad. He could not eat. He could not rest. The secret was eating him from the inside, like a fire.

He began to understand the truth about himself. He was not a great man, above the law. He was just a man — a man who had done a terrible thing and now could not live with it. His theory had been a lie. And the punishment was not prison. The punishment was already here, inside him: this endless fear, this loneliness, this pain that never stopped.
He needed to tell someone. He needed to say the words out loud. And there was only one person he could tell.
Chapter 9. The Confession.
Rodion went to Sonya's room. His face was white. His hands were shaking.
"Sonya," he said. "I have something to tell you. Something terrible."
She looked at him, afraid.
"Do you remember the old woman who was killed?" he said slowly. "And her sister Lizaveta?"
Sonya went pale. "Yes," she whispered.
Rodion could not say the words directly. He looked at her, and his eyes told her the truth before his mouth did.
"It was you," Sonya breathed. "You... killed them."
For a moment there was silence. Then Sonya did something Rodion did not expect. She did not run away. She did not scream. She threw her arms around him and held him close.
"Oh, what have you done to yourself?" she cried. "There is no one in the whole world as unhappy as you now!"
Rodion had thought she would hate him. Instead, she cried for him. She held him and shared his pain. In that moment, he understood that he was not completely alone after all.

"You must do something," Sonya said, looking into his eyes. "Go to the crossroads. Bow down. Kiss the earth that you have hurt. And then tell everyone, out loud: 'I did it.' Confess. Accept your punishment. It is the only way. Only then can you begin to live again."
"They will send me to prison," Rodion said. "To Siberia. For many years."
"Then I will go with you," Sonya said simply. "I will follow you."
Rodion looked at her. He was not ready yet. He was still afraid. But her words stayed in his heart like a small light in the dark.

Meanwhile, Svidrigailov had heard everything through the wall. Now he knew Rodion's secret. For a while he thought about using it. But Svidrigailov was a lost man too, with no love in his life and no hope in his heart. Dunya refused him. His darkness swallowed him. One grey morning, alone and empty, he took his own life.
Chapter 10. A New Life.
The secret could not stay hidden forever.

Rodion walked through the streets one last time. He thought about his mother, his sister, and Sonya. He thought about Lizaveta, gentle and innocent, who had died for nothing. He thought about the man he had wanted to be, and the man he really was.

He came to the crossroads in the middle of the city. He remembered Sonya's words. He knelt down and kissed the dirty ground, while people stared and laughed at him. He did not care. Something in him was breaking open.
Then he walked to the police station. His heart was pounding. Sonya waited outside, watching him with love and fear.
Rodion stood before the officer. For a moment, no words came. He almost turned to leave. But he saw Sonya's face through the door.
He turned back.
"It was I," he said, in a clear voice. "I killed the old woman and her sister Lizaveta, with an axe."
At last, the words were out. The long, heavy secret was gone. He felt weak, and yet, in a strange way, lighter than he had felt in months.
The court sent Rodion to Siberia, to a prison camp far away in the cold. He was given eight years.

And Sonya kept her promise. She left everything behind and followed him. She found a small room near the prison. Every day, she came to see him. The other prisoners loved her, because she was gentle and kind to everyone.

At first, Rodion was cold and silent, even to Sonya. His heart was still hard and proud. He was still not truly sorry inside; he was only sorry that he had failed. His illness returned, and he lay in the prison hospital for a time.
But slowly, something changed.

One clear morning, near the great river, Rodion saw Sonya coming toward him. He looked at her thin, tired, loving face. And suddenly, all his pride and coldness melted away. He fell at her feet and wept. He knew, at last, that he loved her. And with that love, hope came into his heart for the first time.
His punishment was not over. He still had many years in Siberia. But he was no longer alone, and he was no longer lost. He picked up Sonya's old Bible and, for the first time, he wanted to read it.
The old Rodion — the proud young man with the terrible idea — was gone. A new man was slowly being born. His real story, the story of becoming a new person, was only just beginning.
The End.
Chapter 1. The Man Who Read Too Many Books.

In a village in a part of Spain called La Mancha, there lived an old gentleman named Alonso Quixano. He was thin and tall, about fifty years old. He was not rich, but he had enough to live on. He had a house, a housekeeper, a young niece, and a lot of free time.

Alonso loved books — but only one kind of book. He loved old stories about knights. In these stories, brave knights rode across the land, fought giants and monsters, saved beautiful ladies, and won great glory. Alonso read these books all day and all night. He forgot to eat. He forgot to sleep. He sold parts of his land just to buy more books.
Slowly, something strange happened to Alonso's mind. He began to believe that the stories were true. He believed that knights, giants, and magic were real, and that the world still needed heroes.
And then he had the biggest idea of his life.
"I will become a knight!" he said. "I will ride across Spain. I will fight evil and help people in trouble. I will make my name famous forever!"
His mind was not well. But his heart was full of hope.
Chapter 2. A New Name.
Alonso got ready for his great adventure.

In the corner of his house, he found some very old, rusty armour that had belonged to his grandfather. He cleaned it as well as he could and put it on. It was old and broken, but to Alonso it looked wonderful.
He had a thin, tired old horse. To most people it looked weak and bony. But Alonso looked at it with shining eyes and gave it a grand name: Rocinante.
Then he needed a new name for himself, a name worthy of a great knight. He thought for a long time. At last he chose: Don Quixote of La Mancha.

But every knight in the stories loved a beautiful lady, and did brave things in her honour. So Don Quixote needed a lady too. He remembered a simple farm girl from a nearby village. In real life, she did not know him at all. But in his mind, she became a beautiful, noble princess. He gave her a lovely name: Dulcinea del Toboso.
"Everything I do," he said, "I will do for my lady Dulcinea!"
Now he was ready. Early one morning, without telling anyone, Don Quixote rode away to find adventure.
Chapter 3. Sancho Panza.
Don Quixote soon decided that every great knight needs a squire — a helper who travels with him.
He knew a simple, kind farmer from his village named Sancho Panza. Sancho was short and round, with a good heart and a love of food and sleep. He was not clever, but he had a lot of common sense.

Don Quixote made Sancho a promise. "Come with me, Sancho," he said. "Be my squire. If you help me, one day I will win a great island, and I will make you the governor of it. You will be rich and important!"
Sancho thought about his poor life and his empty pockets. An island! A governor! It sounded wonderful.
"All right, sir," Sancho said. "I will come with you."
So Sancho got on his little grey donkey, and the two men rode off together — the tall, thin knight on his bony horse, and the short, round squire on his donkey.
They were a strange pair. Don Quixote saw a world of magic and heroes. Sancho saw the real world of dust, hunger, and hard ground. But they became true friends, and they never left each other.
Chapter 4. The Giants.
One day, they came to a wide, open field. In the field stood about thirty windmills, turning slowly in the wind.
Don Quixote's eyes grew wide. "Look, Sancho!" he cried. "Look at those terrible giants! They have long arms. I will fight them all. Killing such evil giants is good and holy work!"
Sancho looked. "Sir," he said carefully, "those are not giants. They are windmills. Those long arms are just the sails that turn in the wind."
"You know nothing about adventures," said Don Quixote. "You are afraid. Stay back if you wish. I will fight them alone."
He pointed his long spear forward and shouted, "Do not run away, you cowards!" Then he kicked poor Rocinante and rode straight at the nearest windmill.

He pushed his spear into one of the great turning sails. But the wind was strong. The sail swung round, lifted the spear, and threw Don Quixote and his horse high into the air. They crashed down hard onto the ground.
Sancho hurried over. "Oh, sir! I told you they were windmills!"

Don Quixote lay on the ground, hurt and dusty. But he was not sad. "A wicked magician turned the giants into windmills at the last moment," he said, "just to take away my victory. But do not worry, Sancho. In the end, my sword will win."
Sancho helped his friend stand up. This was only the first of many adventures — and many falls.
Chapter 5. The Castle That Was an Inn.
That evening, tired and hungry, they came to a simple country inn.
But Don Quixote did not see an inn. He saw a great castle, with high towers and strong walls. He believed the innkeeper was a lord of the castle, and the ordinary women there were fine ladies.
He spoke to everyone in a grand, old-fashioned way. The people at the inn laughed at him, but they played along for fun.

Don Quixote asked the innkeeper to make him an official knight. The innkeeper, enjoying the joke, agreed. That night, in a silly ceremony, he tapped Don Quixote on the shoulder and named him a true knight.
Don Quixote was overjoyed. Now, in his mind, he was a real, official knight of the road.

But real life was harder than the stories. When it was time to pay or to fight, things went wrong. Don Quixote and Sancho were often beaten, laughed at, and thrown out. Again and again, the two friends left a place hurt and bruised — but Don Quixote's spirit never broke.
Chapter 6. The Armies and the Golden Helmet.
The adventures continued, each one stranger than the last.
One day, Don Quixote saw two large clouds of dust coming toward each other across the plain. "Sancho!" he cried. "Those are two great armies, coming to fight a war! I must help the good side!"
"Sir," said Sancho, "I only see sheep. Two big flocks of sheep, and the dust from their feet."

But Don Quixote would not listen. He rode into the middle of the sheep, waving his spear and shouting like a soldier in battle. The frightened shepherds threw stones at him to save their animals. The stones hit Don Quixote hard, and he fell off his horse, losing some teeth.

Another time, they saw a man riding in the rain, wearing a shiny metal thing on his head to stay dry. It was really just a barber's brass basin — a bowl. But Don Quixote was sure it was a famous golden helmet, worn by great knights long ago.

"That is a magic golden helmet!" he said. He chased the frightened barber away and proudly put the brass bowl on his own head. From that day, he wore the barber's basin as his precious "golden helmet," and nothing could change his mind.
Sancho only shook his head and smiled. He loved his master, even though his master was clearly mad.
Chapter 7. Setting the Prisoners Free.
One day, they met a line of men in chains. Guards were taking them to prison to be punished for their crimes.
Don Quixote stopped and spoke to the prisoners. Each one told him a sad story. Don Quixote's heart was filled with pity. In his mind, a good knight must always help people who are suffering.
"These poor men are being forced against their will," he said. "A true knight must set them free!"
Sancho was worried. "Sir, these are criminals! The king himself sent them to prison. We should not stop the guards."
But Don Quixote did not listen. He attacked the guards and broke the prisoners' chains. The prisoners ran away, free.

But there was no reward. The freed criminals were not grateful. They threw stones at Don Quixote and Sancho, took some of their things, and ran off laughing. Once again, the two friends were left alone, hurt and robbed.
Don Quixote's dreams were beautiful. But the real world did not work the way his books said it should.
Chapter 8. Trying to Bring Him Home.

Back in the village, Don Quixote's friends were very worried. The priest and the barber, who knew him well, wanted to bring him home safely. They were sad to see a good, gentle man lose his mind like this.
They tried different tricks to catch him and take him back. Once, they even put him in a cage and told him a magician had captured him, so he would come home quietly.

For a while, Don Quixote stayed at home and seemed better. But soon the dream called to him again, and he and Sancho rode out for more adventures. Don Quixote could not stop being a knight. It was who he wanted to be.

Sancho, too, kept dreaming of his island. And at one point, some rich people who wanted to laugh at the pair actually did make Sancho the "governor" of a small town, as a joke. But being a governor was hard and full of problems. Sancho was honest and fair, but he soon grew tired of it. "I was born a simple farmer," he said, "and a simple farmer I want to be." He happily gave up the job and went back to his master. He had learned that his dream was not as sweet as it looked.
Chapter 9. The Knight of the White Moon.
Don Quixote's friend, a clever young man named Samson Carrasco, had an idea to cure him.
Samson knew that Don Quixote followed the rules of knights very seriously. In the stories, if one knight beat another in a fair fight, the loser had to obey the winner's commands.
So Samson dressed up in shining armour and called himself "The Knight of the White Moon." He rode up to Don Quixote and challenged him to a fight.
"If I win," said the Knight of the White Moon, "you must go home and stop being a knight for one whole year."
Don Quixote, brave as always, agreed at once.
They fought. But Samson was younger and stronger. He knocked Don Quixote to the ground.
"You have lost," said the Knight of the White Moon. "Now keep your promise."
Don Quixote lay in the dust, beaten. His heart was broken, but his honour would not let him break his word.
"I have lost," he said quietly. "I will keep my promise. I will go home."
Slowly, sadly, the great knight and his faithful squire turned toward home.
Chapter 10. Coming Home.
The journey home was quiet. Don Quixote was tired and sad. His dream of being a hero was over.
When he reached his village, he became ill and had to go to bed. He grew weaker each day.

Then, one morning, something changed. He woke up, and his mind was clear again. The madness was gone. He was no longer Don Quixote, the knight of giants and magic. He was simply Alonso Quixano, a gentle old man.

He looked back at all his adventures and understood them for what they were. "I was foolish," he said softly to his friends around the bed. "Those books filled my head with nonsense. There are no giants, no magic helmets. I see clearly now."
His friends were happy that his mind was well again. But they were also sad, because they could see he was dying.
Sancho stood by the bed with tears in his eyes. "Please don't die, master," he said. "Get up! Let's go on more adventures. Maybe we'll find the lady Dulcinea!"
Don Quixote smiled gently at his good friend. He thanked Sancho for his love and his loyalty. Then, calm and peaceful and sane at last, the good old man closed his eyes and died.

He had been a foolish knight who fought windmills and lost every battle. But he had also been a man who believed in goodness, who dreamed of a better world, and who never stopped trying to help others. And perhaps that is a kind of greatness too.
His friends wept for him. And people still remember the tall, thin knight and his short, faithful squire, riding across the plains of Spain, chasing impossible dreams.
The End.
Chapter 1. Lost in the Dark Forest.
In the middle of his life, a man named Dante found himself lost.

He was walking through a dark, thick forest. He did not know how he had come there. He had left the right path somewhere, and now he was afraid. The trees were black. There was no light. His heart was full of fear.

Dante tried to find his way out. Ahead, he saw a hill with sunlight on top. He wanted to climb it and escape the dark. But three wild animals blocked his way: a leopard, a lion, and a hungry wolf. They were terrible to see. The animals pushed him back, down into the dark valley again.
Dante was trapped. He could not go forward. He could not escape. He felt hopeless.
Then, in the shadows, he saw the shape of a man.
"Help me!" Dante cried. "Please help me, whoever you are!"
Chapter 2. The Guide.
The man in the shadows spoke.
"I am Virgil," he said. "Long ago, I was a poet in ancient Rome. I have come to help you. You cannot pass these wild animals. But do not be afraid. I will show you another way."
Dante knew the name Virgil. He was a great and famous poet from the past. Dante was amazed and grateful.
"A lady in Heaven sent me to you," Virgil said. "Her name is Beatrice. She loves you, and she is worried about your soul. She asked me to guide you to safety."
Dante's heart filled with hope. Beatrice was a woman he had loved deeply. She had died, and now she lived in Heaven. And she still cared about him.

"But the way will be strange and hard," Virgil warned. "To reach the light, we must first travel through dark places. We will go down into Hell, then up the mountain of Purgatory, and at last into Heaven. Are you ready to follow me?"
Dante was frightened. But he trusted Virgil. "Yes," he said. "Lead the way."
Chapter 3. The Gate of Hell.
Virgil led Dante to a great gate. Above the gate were terrible words, carved in stone.
The words said: "Give up all hope, you who enter here."
Dante shivered. But Virgil took his hand. "Be brave," he said. "Here we will see the souls of people who did evil in their lives and never felt sorry. Watch, and learn."
They stepped through the gate.
Inside, the air was full of noise — crying, shouting, and screaming. Dante heard the voices of countless souls in pain. It was dark and full of sadness.
"These people chose evil in their lives," Virgil explained. "Now they must live with what they chose, forever."

Hell was shaped like a giant hole in the earth. It went down and down, in great circles, deeper and deeper. Each circle held a different kind of sinner. And as they went lower, the sins became worse, and the punishments became more terrible.
Dante and Virgil began to walk down into the dark.
Chapter 4. The Lovers in the Wind.
In one of the first circles, Dante saw a great storm. A powerful wind blew without stopping. In the wind, souls were flying, unable to rest, blown here and there forever.
"Who are these souls?" Dante asked.
"These are people who let love become the ruler of their lives, and did wrong because of it," Virgil said. "Now the wind carries them, just as their strong feelings carried them in life."

Two souls flew close together, side by side. Dante called to them, and they came. It was a woman named Francesca and a man named Paolo. They had fallen in love, but it was a forbidden love, and it had ended in death.
Francesca told Dante her sad story with a gentle, tired voice. She spoke of how their love had begun, softly and quietly, and how it had destroyed them both.
Dante listened. His heart broke for them. Their story was so sad that Dante fainted and fell to the ground, overcome with pity.
When he woke, he understood something. The people in Hell were not monsters. They were once ordinary people, like him, who had made terrible choices.
Chapter 5. Deeper and Darker.
Dante and Virgil went deeper into Hell. In each new circle, they saw a new kind of sinner and a new kind of pain.

They saw greedy people who had loved money too much, pushing heavy weights forever. They saw angry people fighting in a dirty, black river. They saw people who had lied and cheated, punished in horrible ways.

Dante noticed something. Each punishment matched the sin. The people who had let their anger burn now fought forever in the mud. The people who had followed their bodies' desires were blown by the endless wind. It was a kind of dark justice: in death, the sinners lived inside their own sins.
The deeper they went, the colder and more terrible it became. Some of the sights were so awful that Dante could hardly look. But Virgil stayed close and kept him safe.
"Do not be afraid," Virgil said again and again. "You are only a visitor here. You will not stay. Keep walking."
Chapter 6. The Bottom of Hell.
At last, they reached the very bottom of Hell. It was not fire, as Dante had expected. It was ice.
The lowest part of Hell was a frozen lake. In the ice were the worst sinners of all: the traitors — people who had betrayed those who trusted and loved them.

And in the very centre stood a giant, terrible figure, frozen in the ice up to his chest. It was Satan himself, the source of all evil. He had three faces and huge wings. He was crying, and his wings made a cold wind that froze the lake around him.
Dante was filled with horror.
"This is the end of the dark journey," Virgil said quietly. "There is nothing lower than this. From here, we can only go up."
Carefully, Virgil and Dante climbed down along Satan's frozen body, and then through a narrow passage in the rock. They climbed and climbed for a long time.
And then, far above, Dante saw something he had not seen in a long time.
Stars.
Chapter 7. The Mountain of Hope.
Dante and Virgil came out onto the shore of a great mountain. The air was fresh and clean. The sky was soft with morning light. After the darkness of Hell, it felt like a beautiful dream.

"This is the mountain of Purgatory," Virgil said. "It is very different from Hell. The souls here also did wrong in their lives. But these souls felt truly sorry. So they are not punished forever. Instead, they are cleaning their souls, step by step, and climbing toward Heaven."

Dante watched the souls on the mountain. They were working hard and suffering, yes — but they were full of hope. They knew that their pain would end. They knew that one day they would reach Heaven. They sang and prayed as they climbed.
"In Hell, there was no hope," Dante said. "Here, there is nothing but hope."
"Yes," said Virgil. "That is the difference. Now, let us climb."
Chapter 8. Cleaning the Soul.
The mountain had many levels. On each level, souls worked to clean away a different weakness.
On one level were the proud people, who had thought too much of themselves in life. Now they walked bent low under heavy stones, learning to be humble.
On another level were people who had been jealous, and people who had been lazy, and people who had wanted too much. Each group worked to become better and to leave their old faults behind.

It was hard work. But every soul climbed higher and higher, growing lighter and cleaner as they went. As Dante climbed with them, he too felt himself becoming lighter, as if a weight was leaving his own heart.
At last, they reached the very top of the mountain. Here was a beautiful garden, full of flowers, trees, and a clear river. It was like the first perfect garden of the world.
But now Virgil stopped. He could not go any further.
"My friend," Virgil said gently, "here I must leave you. I can guide you through Hell and up this mountain. But I cannot enter Heaven. That is not for me. From here, another guide will lead you."
Dante was sad to lose his friend and guide. But he understood. He thanked Virgil for everything, and Virgil quietly went away.
Chapter 9. Beatrice.
Then, in the beautiful garden, Dante saw her.
Beatrice.
She was the woman he had loved so many years ago, the woman who had sent Virgil to save him. Now she stood before him, shining with light, more beautiful than ever.

At first, Beatrice spoke to Dante seriously. She reminded him of his mistakes, of the times he had left the right path in life. Dante felt ashamed and cried. But it was a good kind of crying — the crying of a person who truly wants to be better.
When his heart was clean, Beatrice smiled at him with great love. "Now," she said, "come with me. I will show you Heaven."
She took Dante upward, higher than the mountain, higher than the clouds, up into the sky itself. They rose together toward the stars.
Chapter 10. The Great Light.
Heaven was made of light and love.

Beatrice led Dante up through the shining heavens. Everywhere there were happy souls, full of peace and joy. These were people who had lived good lives, or who had cleaned their souls. Now they lived in perfect happiness, close to God. Every soul was full of love, and the higher Dante rose, the brighter and more beautiful everything became.
The light grew stronger and stronger. It was not painful. It was warm and wonderful. Dante felt his heart filling with a joy he had never known.
At last, Beatrice brought him to the very highest place of all. And there, Dante saw the greatest sight in the universe: a vision of God, a light brighter than a thousand suns, full of endless love.

The sight was too great for words. Dante could not fully understand it, and he could not fully describe it. But in that moment, he felt something perfect and complete. He felt the love that holds the whole universe together — the love that moves the sun and all the stars.

Dante's long journey was over. He had travelled through darkness and fear, through Hell and up the mountain, and at last into the light. He had started lost and afraid in a dark forest. Now his soul was full of peace, hope, and love.
He had found his way home.
The End.
Chapter 1. Two Kinds of Family.
Happy families are all alike. But every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
This is a story about love. It is about two very different loves, and where they lead.
In Russia, long ago, there lived a beautiful woman named Anna Karenina. Everyone who met her loved her. She was warm, kind, and full of life. Her eyes were bright, and her smile lit up every room.

Anna was married to a man named Karenin. He was much older than her. He was an important government official — serious, cold, and correct in everything he did. He was not a bad man, but he was more interested in his work and his good name than in love.
Anna and Karenin had a young son named Seryozha. Anna loved her little boy more than anything in the world.

From the outside, Anna's life looked perfect. She had money, beauty, a respected husband, and a lovely child. But inside, something was missing. Anna had never truly felt deep, passionate love. She did not even know that she wanted it — until the day she met a certain young man.
Chapter 2. The Meeting.
One day, Anna travelled by train to the city of Moscow. At the station, she met a young army officer named Count Vronsky.
Vronsky was handsome, charming, and full of energy. When he looked at Anna, something happened between them. It was quick and powerful, like a spark. Neither of them could forget it.
That night, at a grand ball, they saw each other again. They danced. Everyone in the room could see it: these two people were falling in love.
Anna was frightened by her own feelings. She was a married woman. She had a husband and a son. This was wrong. So she left Moscow and hurried home, trying to run away from what she felt.
But on the train home, Vronsky appeared again. He had followed her.
"I had to see you," he said. "I cannot help it. Where you are, that is where I want to be."
Anna's heart beat fast. She told him to stop. But secretly, she was happy. And she knew, deep down, that her quiet life was over.
Chapter 3. Kitty and Levin.
At the same time, there was another love story happening.
There was a good, honest man named Levin. He was not a city man. He loved the countryside, his farm, and simple, real things. He was thoughtful and a little shy.
Levin was in love with a young woman named Kitty. Kitty was sweet, pretty, and kind. Levin came to the city and asked Kitty to marry him.
But Kitty said no.

Why? Because at that time, Kitty was in love with someone else — the handsome Count Vronsky. She thought Vronsky would marry her. So she turned down the good, honest Levin, and he went home to his farm with a broken heart.
But then Vronsky met Anna. He forgot all about Kitty. He only wanted Anna now.
So poor Kitty was left with nothing. Vronsky did not want her, and she had said no to Levin. She became sad and ill. She had chosen the exciting man over the good man, and it had hurt her badly.
Chapter 4. A Dangerous Love.
Anna tried to be a good wife. But her love for Vronsky grew stronger every day. And Vronsky loved her completely. They began to meet in secret.
People in society started to talk. They whispered behind their hands. "Have you seen Anna and Count Vronsky together? A married woman! How shocking!"
Anna's husband, Karenin, noticed too. He was not really jealous in his heart, but he was worried about his good name.
"People are talking about you and Vronsky," he told Anna coldly. "You must stop. Think of our family. Think of what people will say."
But Anna could not stop. Her love was too strong. For the first time in her life, she felt truly alive, truly loved. She did not want to give that up, even though she knew it was dangerous.
She had to make a terrible choice: her safe life, her good name, and her beloved son — or her love for Vronsky.
Chapter 5. The Choice.
In the end, Anna could not hide her heart any longer.
She told her husband the truth. "I love Vronsky," she said. "I cannot live a lie. I am going to be with him."
Karenin was shocked and hurt. But most of all, he was worried about shame. He did not want the world to know his wife had left him.

The hardest part was Seryozha, her son. If Anna left, she might lose her little boy forever. Karenin was angry, and he could keep the child away from her. This thought broke Anna's heart. But her love for Vronsky pulled her forward.
Anna made her choice. She left her husband. She went to live with Vronsky.
For a while, they were happy. They travelled together. They had a baby daughter. Anna felt she had finally chosen love and freedom.
But she would soon learn the price of that choice.
Chapter 6. Closed Doors.
When Anna and Vronsky returned to society, the doors were closed to her.

The same people who had once loved Anna now turned their backs on her. Women who used to smile at her now looked away. She was not invited to parties. When she walked into a room, people grew silent and cold.
Why? Because Anna had broken the rules. She had left her husband for another man. In their world, that made her a bad woman.

The strange thing was this: many of these same people did secret, wrong things themselves. But they hid them. Anna's only "crime" was that she had been honest and open about her love. And for that, society punished her.
Vronsky could still go anywhere. Men were forgiven for such things. But Anna, the woman, was pushed out and alone.

Worst of all, she almost never saw her son. Once, she secretly visited Seryozha on his birthday. The little boy hugged her and cried. But she had to leave again. The pain of losing her child never left her heart.
Anna was rich in love, but poor in everything else. And slowly, the loneliness began to hurt her.
Chapter 7. A Better Path.
While Anna's life grew darker, another life grew brighter.

Levin, the honest farmer, had never stopped loving Kitty. And Kitty, after her illness and sadness, had grown wiser. She now saw that the good, kind Levin was worth far more than the exciting Vronsky had been.
When Levin and Kitty met again, they understood each other at last. Levin asked Kitty to marry him a second time.
This time, Kitty said yes.

They married, and they went to live together in the peaceful countryside. Their life was not always easy. They argued sometimes, like all couples. They faced hard times, sickness, and worry. But they built their life on real love, trust, and honesty.
Levin and Kitty were learning what Anna could not find: that true happiness is not made of wild passion alone. It is made of loyalty, patience, family, and quiet, everyday love.
Two loves, two very different paths.
Chapter 8. Love Turns to Fear.
Back in the city, Anna and Vronsky's love was changing.
At first, their love had been like a fire. But now the fire was burning them.

Anna had given up everything for Vronsky — her husband, her son, her place in the world. So now she needed Vronsky to be everything to her. She watched him closely. She worried all the time. "Does he still love me?" she asked herself. "Will he leave me too?"
She became jealous. When Vronsky went out without her, she imagined terrible things. When he was even a little cold, she felt sick with fear.
Vronsky still loved Anna. But he felt trapped. He could not go out or live a normal life without Anna becoming upset. Her fear and jealousy pushed him away, little by little.
They began to argue. The more Anna feared losing him, the more she pushed him away. And the more he pulled away, the more she feared. It was a sad circle, and it grew worse and worse.
Anna was alone, rejected by the world, far from her son, and now afraid of losing the only thing she had left.
Chapter 9. Falling Into Darkness.
Anna's mind began to fall apart.

She could not sleep. She started taking medicine to calm herself, and she took more and more of it. Dark thoughts filled her head. She felt that everyone had left her. She felt that even Vronsky, deep down, must hate her now.
None of this was fully true. But Anna could no longer see clearly. Her sadness had become like a thick fog, and she was lost inside it.
She and Vronsky had a terrible argument. Anna was sure it meant the end. She was sure he would never come back. Her heart was full of pain and hopelessness.
"No one loves me," she thought. "I have lost everything. My son, my home, my good name — and now even Vronsky. What is left for me? Why should I keep living in all this pain?"

In her broken state, one terrible idea filled her mind. She thought that if she died, then Vronsky would be sorry. Then he would understand her pain. It was a sick and hopeless thought, but Anna could not fight it anymore.
Chapter 10. The Station.
Anna went to a train station.
It was the same kind of place where she had first met Vronsky, long ago, when her new life had begun. Now she stood on the platform, watching the great trains come and go.
Her mind was full of dark clouds. She felt cold and empty. All around her, people were living their normal lives, but Anna felt completely alone in the world.
A train came toward the platform, huge and loud.
In her last moments, Anna felt confused and afraid. For one second, she wanted to stop, to take it all back. But it was too late.
Anna threw herself in front of the train.
And so her life ended — a beautiful, loving woman, destroyed not only by her own choices, but by a cruel world that would not forgive her for loving.
When Vronsky learned what had happened, he was crushed with grief and guilt. He had lost her forever. Broken and empty, he went off to war, no longer caring whether he lived or died.
Chapter 11. Peace.
And what of Levin, the honest farmer?
Levin's life was quiet, but it was full. He and Kitty had a baby son now. Levin loved his family and his land.

But Levin had his own struggles too — not with love, but with big questions. He often asked himself: What is the meaning of life? Why are we here? What is good? For a long time, these questions troubled him deeply, and he could not find peace.

Then, slowly, watching his wife, his child, and the simple people who worked on his land, Levin began to understand. The answer was not in clever ideas or great passions. The answer was in living a good, honest life. It was in loving other people, doing your work well, and being kind each day.
Levin found his peace not in the head, but in the heart.
Two people had looked for happiness. Anna had chased a burning passion, and it had destroyed her in a cruel world. Levin had built a quiet love, day by day, and it had saved him.

Their two stories, side by side, show us something important about the human heart: that love can lift us up to the light, or pull us down into the dark — and that true happiness is often found in the simple, faithful, everyday things we might forget to notice.
The End.
Chapter 1. The Man in the Graveyard.
My name is Pip. This is the story of my life, and of a great mistake I made about what really matters.

When I was a small boy, I was an orphan. My parents were dead. I lived with my older sister, who was hard and often angry. But her husband, Joe Gargery, was a good, gentle man. Joe was a blacksmith — he made things from iron. Joe was poor and simple, but he loved me like a father, and I loved him.

One cold evening, I went to the graveyard near the marshes. Suddenly, a frightening man jumped out from behind a stone. His clothes were dirty and torn, and there was a heavy iron chain on his leg. He was an escaped prisoner.
"Be quiet!" the man said, grabbing me. "Bring me food. And bring me a file, to cut this iron off my leg. Do it, or I will hurt you! And tell no one!"
I was terrified. "Yes, sir," I said.
Chapter 2. Helping the Prisoner.

That night, I could not sleep. Early in the morning, while everyone was asleep, I took some food from the kitchen — bread, cheese, and meat. I also took a file from Joe's workshop. Then I ran to the marshes.
I found the prisoner, cold and shaking. He ate the food quickly, like a hungry animal. I felt afraid, but I also felt sorry for him.
"Thank you, boy," he said quietly. He looked at me in a strange way, as if he would remember me forever.

Later, soldiers caught the prisoner again and took him away in chains. As they took him, he told the soldiers that he had stolen the food himself. He did this to protect me, so I would not get in trouble. It was a small kindness, and I did not forget it.
I thought I would never see that man again. I was wrong. And that one act of kindness would change my whole life — but I would not understand how for many years.
Chapter 3. The Strange House.
Some time later, something unusual happened. A very rich old woman named Miss Havisham wanted a boy to come and visit her big house and keep her company. My family chose me.
Miss Havisham's house was dark and strange. All the clocks were stopped at the same time — twenty minutes to nine. The curtains were always closed.

And Miss Havisham herself was the strangest sight of all. She was old, but she wore a wedding dress, yellow with age. She wore only one shoe. On the table was an old wedding cake, covered in dust and spiders.

Many years before, Miss Havisham had been going to get married. But on her wedding day, the man left her. Her heart broke. From that moment, she stopped all the clocks and never changed her dress. She stayed in the dark with her broken heart, hating all men.
In the house also lived a beautiful young girl named Estella. She was about my age, with lovely eyes and a cold, proud face.
"Play with the boy, Estella," said Miss Havisham.
But Estella looked at me with cold eyes. "He is just a common working boy," she said. "Look at his rough hands and his heavy boots." She laughed at me.
Chapter 4. Ashamed.
I fell in love with Estella. Even though she was cruel to me, I could not stop thinking about her. She was beautiful, and I wanted her to like me.

But Estella made me feel ashamed. For the first time, I looked at my own life and felt embarrassed. I was poor. My hands were rough from work. Joe was only a simple blacksmith. Before, I had been happy. Now, next to Estella, I felt low and common.

What I did not know then was this: Miss Havisham had raised Estella for one purpose. Her heart was broken by a man, so she taught Estella to break men's hearts too. She trained Estella to be cold and to make men love her, and then to hurt them. Estella could not really love anyone. It was very sad, but I could not see it then.
I began to wish for a different life. "I want to be a gentleman," I thought. "A rich, educated man with fine clothes. Then Estella will love me. Then I will be good enough."
I was becoming ashamed of the good, honest life I had. And I did not yet understand what a terrible mistake that was.
Chapter 5. Great Expectations.
A few years passed. I was learning to be a blacksmith, working with Joe. But my heart was not in it. I still dreamed of being a gentleman.
Then, one day, a serious London lawyer named Mr. Jaggers came to see me. He had amazing news.

"Pip," he said, "you have great expectations. A secret person, who wishes to remain unknown, has given you a large amount of money. You will go to London. You will become a gentleman. You will have a fine education and everything you need. But you must never ask who your secret helper is."
I could not believe it! My dream was coming true! I was going to be rich. I was going to be a gentleman.
In my heart, I was sure I knew who the secret person was. It must be Miss Havisham, I thought. She was rich. And surely she was planning for me to marry Estella one day! It all seemed perfect.
I was so excited about my new life that I forgot the most important things.
Chapter 6. The Gentleman.
I went to London. I bought fine clothes. I learned the manners of a gentleman. I spent money freely.
But something bad happened to me. As I became richer, I became worse.
I became a snob. I started to feel that my old life was low and shameful. And, worst of all, I became ashamed of dear Joe — kind, loving Joe, who had been like a father to me.

Once, Joe came to London to visit me. But I was cold to him. I was embarrassed by his simple clothes and country manners. I made him feel unwelcome. Poor Joe understood, and he left quietly and sadly.
"Goodbye, Pip, old friend," Joe said gently. He was not angry. He was just hurt.
I knew, deep inside, that I was behaving badly. But I did not stop. My new money and my dreams of Estella had made me forget who I really was and who really loved me.
I was a gentleman on the outside. But inside, I was becoming a poor kind of man.
Chapter 7. The Secret Revealed.
Then, one stormy night, everything changed.
There was a knock at my door. An old man came in — rough, grey, and tired. At first I did not know him. Then I looked closer, and my blood went cold.
It was the prisoner. The frightening man from the graveyard, all those years ago. The man I had given food and a file.
"Hello, Pip, my boy," he said, with tears in his eyes and a warm smile. "Do you not know me?"

His name was Magwitch. He told me his story. After that day in the marshes, he had been sent far away to Australia. There, he had worked hard for many years and become rich. But he had never forgotten the poor boy who once helped him.

"You gave me food when I was hungry and afraid," Magwitch said. "You were kind to me. So I decided to make you rich. Every penny of your money — it came from me. I made you a gentleman, Pip. You are my gentleman."

I felt sick. The truth hit me like a hammer. My money did not come from Miss Havisham. It came from this poor, rough criminal. All my dreams — Miss Havisham, Estella, being a fine gentleman — were built on a lie I had told myself.
And I had been ashamed of good Joe, while a hunted convict had given me everything.
Chapter 8. Learning to Care.
At first, I was horrified. I did not want Magwitch's money. I did not want anything to do with a criminal.

But slowly, as I spent time with him, my feelings changed. I saw that Magwitch was not a monster. He was a man with a big, loving heart. He had suffered greatly in his life. And everything he had done, he had done out of love and gratitude for me.
I began to feel deep shame — not shame of Magwitch, but shame of myself. He had loved me and given me everything. And I had become a selfish snob.

I also learned a shocking secret. Magwitch had once had a little daughter, long ago, whom he thought he had lost. And through Mr. Jaggers, I discovered the truth: that lost daughter was Estella. The cold, beautiful girl I loved was really the daughter of this poor prisoner.

The rich and the poor, the gentleman and the criminal — I began to see that these labels did not show what was really inside a person. Magwitch, the criminal, had a better heart than I, the "gentleman," had shown.
Chapter 9. Danger and Loss.
But Magwitch was in great danger. He had come back to England to see me, and that was against the law for him. If the police found him, he would be put to death.
I decided to help him. It did not matter anymore that he was a criminal. He had loved me, and now I loved him. I had to save him.

We made a secret plan to help Magwitch escape from England by boat. But at the last moment, the plan failed. An old enemy of Magwitch's told the police. As we tried to escape on the river, the police caught us. In the struggle, Magwitch was badly hurt.
Magwitch was arrested and sentenced to death. But he was too sick and injured to be executed. He lay dying in prison.
I stayed by his side. I held his hand. And before he died, I gave him a gift of words.
"Magwitch," I said softly, "your daughter did not die. She is alive. She is a beautiful lady. And I love her."
A peaceful smile came to his face. Then he closed his eyes and died, holding my hand.
I had lost him. But I had also learned to love him. And I was glad I had stayed.
Chapter 10. Coming Home.
When Magwitch died, his money went to the government, as the law said. So I lost my fortune. I was not rich anymore. I was not a fine gentleman anymore.
And you know what? I was almost glad.

I became ill from all the worry and sadness. And when I was sick, someone came to take care of me, day and night, with love and patience. It was Joe. Dear, good Joe, whom I had treated so badly. He had heard I was ill, and he came at once. He never once said an angry word about how I had hurt him.
When I got better, I was filled with shame and love. I went to find Joe and begged him to forgive me.
"Joe," I said, crying, "I am so sorry. I was a fool. You are the best man I have ever known. Please forgive me."
Joe just smiled his gentle smile. "It is all forgotten, Pip, old friend," he said. "We are friends, always."

I had learned the greatest lesson of my life. Being a gentleman was never about money, or fine clothes, or important friends. It was about having a kind and honest heart — a heart like Joe's, and like Magwitch's. I had chased money and status, and they had made me worse. Now, poor again, I felt like a better man.
I went to work honestly, in an ordinary job, and I lived a simple, good life. And I was happy.
Chapter 11. Estella.
Many years passed.
Miss Havisham, before she died, had understood at last the harm she had done. She had made Estella cold, and she had used me, and she was deeply sorry. She had begged me to forgive her, and I did.

As for Estella — her cold life had brought her pain. She married a cruel man, and her marriage was unhappy. Life had been hard for her, and it had changed her. The suffering had melted some of the ice around her heart.
One evening, I walked in the garden of Miss Havisham's old, ruined house. And there, by chance, I met Estella again.
She was older now, and quieter. The cold pride was gone from her eyes. In its place was something softer, something sad and gentle.
"Pip," she said. "After so many years. Can we be friends?"
I looked at her. All the pain of the past was behind us. We had both suffered. We had both learned. We had both changed.
"Yes, Estella," I said. "Friends."

I took her hand, and we walked out of the ruined garden together, into the evening light. The sadness of the past was still with us. But ahead, at last, there seemed to be a little hope — for both of us.
The End.
Chapter 1. The Unwanted Child.
My name is Jane Eyre. I was a small, plain, quiet girl, and for a long time, nobody loved me.

My parents died when I was a baby. So I went to live with my aunt, Mrs. Reed, in her big house. But my aunt did not want me. She was cold and cruel. Her three children were cruel too. They hit me and called me names, and no one ever helped me.

I was lonely and unhappy. But even as a child, I had something strong inside me. I would not simply accept unfair treatment. One day, when my cousin hurt me, I fought back and told my aunt the truth about how badly she treated me.
My aunt was angry. She decided to send me away to a school far from home. In some ways, I was glad. Any place, I thought, must be better than this house where no one loved me.
I was only ten years old, but I was ready to leave. I wanted a life of my own.
Chapter 2. The Cold School.
The school was called Lowood. It was a school for poor girls, and life there was very hard.
The rooms were cold. The food was bad, and there was never enough. The rules were strict, and the man in charge, Mr. Brocklehurst, was unkind. He believed the girls should suffer to become good.
But at Lowood, I found my first real friend. Her name was Helen Burns. Helen was gentle, patient, and wise. When the teachers were cruel to her, she did not become angry. She was calm and forgiving.
"Life is too short for hate, Jane," Helen told me. "It is better to love."
I did not fully understand her then. But I loved her.
That winter, a terrible sickness came to the school. Many girls became ill. And my dear friend Helen became very sick too.
One night, I crept into her bed to be with her.
"I am happy, Jane," Helen whispered. "I am going to a better place. Do not cry."
In the morning, Helen was gone. She had died in the night, in my arms. I never forgot her, or her gentle, loving heart.
Chapter 3. A New Life.
The years passed. Things at Lowood slowly got better. I studied hard, and I grew from a child into a young woman. I stayed at the school and became a teacher myself.
But after some years, I wanted more. I wanted to see the world. So I put an advertisement in the newspaper, looking for work as a governess — a teacher for a rich family's children.
Soon I got a reply. A large house called Thornfield Hall needed a governess for a little girl. I accepted, and I travelled there to begin my new life.
Thornfield was a big, old, grand house. My student was a sweet little French girl named Adèle. The housekeeper was kind. I was happy to be there.

But the house had a secret. High up, on the top floor, I sometimes heard a strange sound — a low, cold laugh. When I asked about it, people told me it was just a servant. But something about it did not feel right.
And I had not yet met the master of the house.
Chapter 4. Mr. Rochester.

One evening, walking on the road, I helped a man whose horse had slipped. He was not handsome. He had a dark, serious face and a rough manner. Later, I learned that this man was Mr. Rochester — the master of Thornfield Hall.
Mr. Rochester was a strange man. He was often moody. Sometimes he was cold, and sometimes he was warm. He asked me many questions and seemed interested in my thoughts.

I was not beautiful, and I was only a poor governess. But Mr. Rochester talked to me as an equal. He liked my honest, direct way of speaking. And slowly, I began to enjoy our conversations very much. When he was away, I missed him.
I did not want to admit it, but I was falling in love with Mr. Rochester.
Still, strange things kept happening in that house, especially at night.
Chapter 5. Fire in the Night.
One night, I woke up because I smelled smoke.
I ran to Mr. Rochester's room. His bed was on fire! Flames were all around him while he slept. Quickly, I threw water on the fire and woke him. I saved his life.
"Who did this?" I asked. "Someone started this fire on purpose!"
Mr. Rochester looked strange and worried. "Say nothing about this to anyone," he told me. "I know who did it. Do not ask questions."
I was confused. Why would he not call for help or ask who tried to kill him? What was he hiding?
More frightening things happened after that. One night, a guest in the house was attacked and hurt. Again, Mr. Rochester kept it quiet. Again, there was that cold laugh from the top floor.
There was a dark secret in Thornfield Hall. I could feel it. But I loved Mr. Rochester, and I trusted him, so I did not push him to tell me.
Chapter 6. The Proposal.
One warm summer evening, Mr. Rochester and I walked in the garden.
Then he surprised me completely.
"Jane," he said, "I want you to be my wife. Will you marry me?"
I could not believe it. A rich man like him, wanting to marry a poor, plain governess like me?
"Are you serious?" I asked. "Do you really love me?"
"I do," he said. "You are strange, and small, and quiet — and I love you more than anyone in the world. You are my equal. Marry me, Jane."
My heart was full of joy. "Yes," I said. "Yes, I will marry you."
I was the happiest I had ever been in my life. Finally, someone loved me. Finally, I had a home and a future.
We planned to marry soon. But I did not know that a terrible secret was about to destroy everything.
Chapter 7. The Secret.
The wedding day came. Mr. Rochester and I stood together in the church. The priest began the ceremony.
But suddenly, a stranger stood up and shouted, "Stop! This wedding cannot happen! Mr. Rochester is already married!"
I felt the world spin around me. Already married?
It was true. Mr. Rochester's face turned grey. Slowly, he told us the terrible secret.

Many years before, he had married a woman named Bertha Mason. But after the wedding, Bertha became very ill in her mind. She lost her reason and became wild and dangerous. She could not live a normal life.
Mr. Rochester did not send her away to a cruel place. Instead, he kept her safely at Thornfield Hall — locked in a room on the top floor, with a servant to care for her.
Now I understood everything. The cold laugh. The fire in the night. The attack. All of it was Bertha, his mad wife, who sometimes escaped from her room.
Mr. Rochester was already married. He could not marry me.
Chapter 8. Jane Must Go.
Mr. Rochester begged me to stay with him anyway.

"I know I cannot legally marry you," he said. "But please, Jane, stay with me. Live with me. I love only you. Bertha is not really my wife anymore — her mind is gone. We can be together. No one needs to know."
I loved him with all my heart. Part of me wanted to say yes. It would have been easy.

But I could not. I had my own beliefs about right and wrong. To stay with him this way would be against my principles. I had to respect myself, even more than I loved him. If I stayed, I would lose the one thing that was truly mine: my own dignity.
"I must go," I said, crying. "I cannot stay. I have to be true to myself."
That night, with a broken heart, I left Thornfield Hall. I took almost nothing. I walked away into the dark, with no home, no money, and no plan.
It was the hardest thing I ever did. But I did it, because I would not give up who I was, even for love.
Chapter 9. Strangers and Family.
I wandered across the wild countryside, cold and hungry. I had no food and nowhere to sleep. I nearly died.
At last, I came to a small house. A kind young man named St. John Rivers and his two sisters took me in. They gave me food, a warm bed, and friendship. Slowly, I grew strong again.
Then two amazing things happened.
First, I learned that an uncle I had never met had died and left me a large amount of money. I was rich now! And I was no longer alone in the world.

Second, and even more surprising, I discovered that St. John and his sisters were actually my cousins — my real family! I was so happy to have a family at last that I shared my new money with them equally.
For the first time, I had a family who loved me. But something was still missing. Every day, I thought about Mr. Rochester. I still loved him.
St. John was a good but cold man. He was planning to travel far away to work as a missionary. He asked me to marry him and go with him — not for love, but to help him in his work.
I almost said yes, out of duty. But I knew, deep down, that a marriage without love was not right for me. I could not do it.
Chapter 10. The Voice.
One quiet evening, as I was thinking hard about what to do, something strange happened.
I heard a voice. It was the voice of Mr. Rochester, calling my name from far away.
"Jane! Jane! Jane!"
It sounded full of pain and love. It was as if his heart was calling to mine across all the miles between us.
I could not explain it. But I knew, in that moment, what I had to do. I had to find Mr. Rochester. I had to know if he was all right.
I said goodbye to my cousins. And I travelled back to Thornfield Hall.
But when I arrived, I found something terrible. Thornfield Hall was gone. It was black and broken, burned to the ground. Only ruined walls were left.
"What happened here?" I asked a local man.

"A great fire," he said. "The master's mad wife started it one night. She died in the flames. Mr. Rochester tried to save her, and to save the servants. He got everyone out. But the house fell on him. He lived — but he lost his sight, and one of his hands. He is blind now. He lives in a small house in the country, all alone."
Chapter 11. Reader, I Married Him.
I hurried to the small house where Mr. Rochester now lived.
I found him there — blind, sad, and lonely. The strong, proud man I had known was quiet and broken now. My heart filled with love and pity.
"Mr. Rochester," I said softly.
He turned his blind eyes toward my voice. "Jane?" he whispered. "Is it really you? No, it cannot be. I must be dreaming."
"It is really me," I said, taking his hand. "I have come back. And I will never leave you again."
He could hardly believe it. "But I am blind now," he said. "I am weak. I have nothing. Why would you stay with a broken man?"

"Because I love you," I said. "And now we are truly equal. His wife had died in the fire, so he was free at last. And I was free too — rich, independent, with a family of my own. I came to him not out of need, but out of pure love.
And so, at last, I married the man I loved.
Reader, I married him.
We lived together in great happiness. I was his eyes, and he was my heart. After some time, he even got a little of his sight back in one eye — enough to see our first child when the baby was born.

I had started as an unwanted, unloved orphan. I had suffered, and I had stayed true to myself through everything. And in the end, I found what I had always wanted most: a home, a family, and a love that was real, and equal, and free.
The End.
Chapter 1. A Party in St. Petersburg.

In the year 1805, the rich and important people of St. Petersburg met at grand parties. They talked about one man above all others: Napoleon, the emperor of France. Some feared him. Some admired him. War between France and Russia was coming, and everyone could feel it.

At one of these parties stood a large, clumsy young man named Pierre Bezukhov. He did not fit in. He said the wrong things and stood in the wrong places. Pierre was the son of a very rich count, but he was not the count's legal son, so he owned nothing and belonged nowhere. Still, people liked something in his honest, open face.

Pierre's best friend was a very different kind of man: Prince Andrei Bolkonsky. Andrei was handsome, clever, and proud. But he was bored and unhappy. He was married to a sweet, pretty wife, yet he felt trapped by his easy life. He wanted something greater.
"I am going to the war," Andrei told Pierre quietly. "I cannot live like this any longer. I want to do something real. I want glory."
Pierre did not understand. "But you have everything," he said.
Andrei only smiled sadly. "Everything and nothing," he replied.
Chapter 2. The Sky Above the Battle.
Prince Andrei went to fight against Napoleon. He dreamed of a great moment — a moment when he would become a hero.

That moment seemed to come at a huge battle. The Russian army was losing. Soldiers were running away in fear. Andrei saw a flag fall to the ground. He picked it up and ran forward, shouting, leading the men.
Then something hit him. He fell.
He lay on his back on the cold field. Above him was the enormous, quiet sky. Clouds moved slowly across it. And suddenly, all his dreams of glory seemed small and foolish.
"How did I never see this sky before?" he thought. "There is nothing but this endless, peaceful sky. Everything else — war, fame, Napoleon — it is all empty. All lies."

Later, Napoleon himself walked across the field and passed the wounded Andrei. Once, Andrei had thought Napoleon was the greatest man in the world. Now the great emperor looked small and unimportant next to that huge, silent sky.
Andrei did not die. He was hurt, but he lived, and slowly he went home — a changed man, tired of dreams of greatness.
Chapter 3. Pierre's Fortune and His Mistake.
While Andrei was at war, Pierre's life changed completely.
His father, the old count, died. And to everyone's surprise, he left his entire fortune to Pierre. Overnight, the clumsy young man who owned nothing became one of the richest men in Russia.
Now everyone wanted to be Pierre's friend. Everyone smiled at him. And a beautiful young woman named Hélène suddenly seemed very interested in him.

Hélène was one of the most beautiful women in the city. But behind her lovely face, she was cold, selfish, and empty. Her family pushed Pierre and Hélène together, and Pierre, confused and lonely, married her.

It was a terrible mistake. Hélène did not love him. She only wanted his money and his name. She lived her own life and made him miserable. Pierre grew jealous and angry. He even fought a duel with a man he believed was Hélène's lover, and almost died.

After that, Pierre left his wife. He was rich, but deeply unhappy. He asked himself the questions that would follow him for years: What is the point of life? What is good? How should a person live? He had no answers, and the emptiness hurt him.
Chapter 4. The Rostov Family.

Not far away lived a warm and noisy family called the Rostovs. They were kind, generous people who loved parties, music, and each other. They were not careful with money, and slowly they were becoming poor — but their house was always full of life.

The youngest daughter was Natasha Rostova. Natasha was not the most beautiful girl, but she was full of energy and joy. She sang, she laughed, she cried easily, and she loved with her whole heart. When Natasha entered a room, everything felt more alive.
Her brother, Nikolai Rostov, was a young soldier, brave and honest, who also went to fight in the war.

Meanwhile, Prince Andrei had returned home to sad news. His gentle young wife had died giving birth to their son. Andrei felt guilty and empty. He had not loved her enough, and now she was gone. He decided he was finished with life and passion. He would just live quietly and raise his child.
But Andrei's cold heart was about to wake up again.
Chapter 5. Natasha and Andrei.
One night, Prince Andrei visited the Rostov house. He was tired and grey inside, sure that happiness was behind him.

Then he heard a young girl's voice at the window above him, talking to the night, so full of life and wonder that it made him ache. It was Natasha. Something in her joy touched the frozen part of his heart.
Later, Andrei saw Natasha at her first grand ball. She was nervous, hoping someone would dance with her. Andrei asked her to dance. As they moved together, both of them felt something warm and new.
Andrei fell in love. For the first time in years, he wanted to live again. And Natasha loved him too — this serious, handsome, wounded man.
Andrei asked Natasha to marry him, and she said yes. They were full of happiness.

But there was one problem. Andrei's father, a hard old prince, did not approve. He made one condition: they must wait one whole year before marrying. Andrei agreed, and then he went away, travelling abroad.
So Natasha had to wait. A year felt like forever to a passionate young girl. She loved Andrei, but he was far away, and she was young, lonely, and impatient.
Chapter 6. The Betrayal.

While she waited, Natasha met a handsome young man named Anatole Kuragin. Anatole was charming, exciting, and completely without honour. He said beautiful words to her, and he made her feel wanted. He was, in fact, Hélène's brother, and just as selfish as his sister.

Natasha was young and her head was turned. Anatole told her he loved her. He said they should run away together and marry in secret. Confused and swept away, Natasha agreed. She wrote to Andrei's family and broke off her engagement.
But it was all a lie. Anatole did not truly love her. Worse, he was already secretly married — he only wanted to use her.
At the last moment, the secret escape was discovered and stopped. The truth came out. Natasha learned that Anatole had tricked her.
She was destroyed. She had thrown away the good, honest love of Andrei for a cruel lie. She felt such shame and pain that she became seriously ill. She even tried to poison herself.
When Andrei returned and heard what had happened, his proud heart turned cold and hard. He could not forgive her. "It is finished," he said.

In her darkest days, one person was gentle and kind to Natasha: Pierre. Pierre had always liked Natasha, and now he felt deep pity and tenderness for her. "If I were free," he thought suddenly, surprising himself, "I would ask for your hand on my knees." He did not say it aloud. But he began to understand that he loved her.
Chapter 7. The War Returns.
In 1812, everything changed. Napoleon led a giant army into Russia. This was not a small, distant war. This was an invasion of the homeland.
The whole country rose up. Young men joined the army. Old men gave money. Everyone was afraid, and everyone was ready to fight for Russia.

Andrei went back to the army, still cold and empty inside, almost hoping to die. Nikolai Rostov fought bravely. And even Pierre, the clumsy thinker, felt he had to do something. He could not just sit in his rich house while his country burned. He decided to go and see the war with his own eyes.
The two great armies moved toward each other. They met near a village called Borodino, not far from Moscow. There they fought one of the most terrible battles in history.
Chapter 8. The Battle of Borodino.
Thousands upon thousands of men fought and died at Borodino. The noise was like the end of the world. Smoke covered the sky. The ground shook.

Pierre wandered onto the battlefield in his ordinary clothes, out of place, unable to look away. He watched simple soldiers fight and fall. He saw their courage and their fear. He was frightened, but he could not leave. He felt he was seeing something true and important about human life and death.
Prince Andrei was there too, with his men, waiting under fire. A shell landed near him and exploded. Andrei was badly, terribly wounded.

The battle did not have a clear winner. Both sides lost enormous numbers of men. But the Russian army, though hurt, was not destroyed. And Napoleon, though he pushed forward, had won nothing that would save him.
The Russian generals made a hard choice. To save the army, they gave up Moscow. They let Napoleon take the ancient city without another great battle.
Chapter 9. Moscow Burns.
Napoleon marched into Moscow, expecting glory. But he found an almost empty city. The people had fled. And then, fires broke out everywhere. Moscow burned.
The French army sat in the ruins of a burning city, with little food and no victory. Napoleon had captured Moscow, but Moscow gave him nothing.

Pierre stayed behind in the burning city. A strange, wild idea had filled his mind: he would find Napoleon and kill him, and so save Russia and become a hero. It was a mad plan, and it failed. Instead, while trying to save a child and a woman from the fire and from French soldiers, Pierre was arrested.

The French took him prisoner. They thought he might be a spy or a criminal. Suddenly, the richest man in Russia was just a dirty prisoner, walking in a line of other prisoners, cold and hungry, waiting to learn if he would be shot.
Chapter 10. The Simple Man.
In prison, Pierre met a simple peasant soldier named Platon Karataev.

Platon owned nothing. He had suffered greatly. Yet he was calm, kind, and somehow happy. He accepted everything that happened — good or bad — without anger or fear. He loved everyone he met. He told simple stories and lived in the present moment.

Watching Platon, Pierre finally understood the answer he had been searching for all his life. Happiness did not come from money, or fame, or clever ideas. It came from a simple, loving, accepting heart. It came from being alive and being part of the world, and from loving other people.

Pierre had lost his freedom, his comfort, and almost his life. But in that terrible prison, he found peace inside himself for the first time. "Life is everything," he thought. "Life is God. To love life is to love God."
It was the hardest and most important lesson of his life.
Chapter 11. Andrei and Natasha, Again.
The wounded Prince Andrei was carried away from Moscow with other injured men. And by chance — or by fate — the family caring for him on the road was the Rostovs, who were fleeing the war.
Natasha discovered that Andrei, the man she had loved and betrayed, was there, dying.
She went to him. She fell on her knees beside him, full of shame and love and sorrow.
"Forgive me," she whispered. "Please forgive me."
And now, close to death, all of Andrei's cold pride was gone. Looking at her, he felt only love — a deep, gentle, forgiving love, not just for Natasha, but for everyone and everything.
"I love you more than before," he told her softly. "Better than before."
Natasha stayed with him. She cared for him day and night. For a short time, they were at peace together, and their love was pure and quiet.

But Andrei's wound was too deep. He grew weaker. He was no longer afraid of death; he felt he understood it now, like a door into something greater. And gently, with Natasha beside him, Prince Andrei died.
Natasha's heart broke. But strangely, her great sorrow also made her wiser and deeper. The silly girl was gone; a woman who understood love and loss remained.
Chapter 12. The Long Retreat.
Winter came. And winter was Russia's greatest weapon.

Napoleon's huge army had to leave the ruins of Moscow. There was no food and no shelter. The Russian cold was deadly. As the French soldiers marched home through the snow, thousands died of hunger and cold. The great army that had invaded Russia fell apart. It became a crowd of frozen, starving men.

The prisoners, including Pierre, were forced to march with them. It was a terrible journey. Many died along the road, including gentle Platon Karataev. Pierre survived, thin and ragged, but with a quiet strength inside him that he had never had before.
At last, Russian soldiers freed the prisoners. Pierre was saved. Napoleon's dream of conquering Russia was completely destroyed. The war was ending.
Chapter 13. Peace.
The war was over. Slowly, life began again.
Pierre returned to Moscow. He was still rich, but he was a new man — calmer, wiser, and kinder. He met Natasha again. She, too, had changed; grief had made her gentle and deep.

The two of them, who had both suffered so much, found in each other a quiet, true happiness. Pierre and Natasha married. And this time, for Pierre, it was real love — nothing like his cold first marriage. (Hélène had died during the war years, and Pierre was free.)
Nikolai Rostov, Natasha's brave brother, married Princess Marya, Andrei's kind and gentle sister. Their two families joined together in love.

Years later, we see them living peaceful, ordinary lives. Pierre and Natasha have children now. Natasha is no longer the wild young girl who danced at the ball; she is a devoted wife and mother, happy in her simple family life. Pierre still thinks about big questions — about goodness, about how people should live — but now he is grounded in love and family.

They had lived through war, betrayal, death, and loss. They had chased glory and money and passion, and found them empty. And in the end, what remained was the simplest and greatest thing of all: to love other people, and to be alive.
That was the peace they had all been searching for.
The End.
Chapter 1. A Bad Father.

In a small Russian town lived a man named Fyodor Karamazov. He was rich, but he was not a good man. He was greedy, cruel, and selfish. He drank too much, laughed at serious things, and cared about no one but himself.

Fyodor had been married twice, and he had three sons. But he was a terrible father. He never took care of his children. When they were small, he sent them away and almost forgot about them. Other people had to raise them.

The three sons grew up far from their father and from each other. As men, they came back to the town, and their lives crossed again. They were three completely different people. And soon, a dark event would tie them all together forever.
Chapter 2. The Three Brothers.

The oldest son was Dmitri, but everyone called him Mitya. Dmitri was a soldier — wild, passionate, and full of strong feelings. He could be generous one moment and violent the next. He loved life, women, and wine, and he spent money quickly. He had a big heart, but he had no control over himself.

The second son was Ivan. Ivan was clever and cold. He read many books and thought deep, difficult thoughts. He did not believe in God. He looked at all the pain and cruelty in the world and asked, "How can there be a loving God when children suffer?" Ivan kept his feelings hidden, but inside, his mind was troubled and dark.

The youngest son was Alyosha. Alyosha was gentle, kind, and loving. Everyone trusted him. He believed in God with his whole heart and lived in the local monastery as a young monk. He did not judge people; he simply loved them. Alyosha was the good and peaceful centre of the family.

There was also a fourth young man in the house. His name was Smerdyakov, and he was the servant. Many people whispered that Smerdyakov was secretly another son of old Fyodor, born to a poor woman. Smerdyakov was quiet, strange, and full of hidden anger. He suffered from a sickness that sometimes made him fall down in fits. He watched the family with cold eyes and said little.
Chapter 3. The Wise Old Monk.
Alyosha loved and followed a wise old monk called Elder Zosima. Zosima was famous in the region. People travelled far to ask him for advice and comfort.

Zosima taught a simple but powerful message: love everyone and everything. He said that every person is responsible, not only for their own actions, but in some way for everyone else too. "Each of us is guilty before all, for everyone and everything," he said. If we truly understood this, he taught, we would fill the world with love instead of cruelty.
Alyosha believed these words deeply. He wanted to bring a little of that love into his broken, angry family.

One day, old Zosima did something surprising. In front of everyone, he bowed low to the ground before Dmitri, the wild oldest brother. No one understood why. Later, people believed the old monk had seen the great suffering that was coming to Dmitri, and had bowed to that suffering.
Soon after, Elder Zosima died. Alyosha was left alone to face the storm gathering in his family.
Chapter 4. Money and a Woman.
Two things brought Dmitri and his father Fyodor into terrible conflict: money and a woman.
