First, the money. Dmitri believed his father was keeping money that belonged to him from his dead mother. He needed it badly, because he had debts. But old Fyodor refused to give him a single coin. They argued again and again, shouting and threatening.

Second, the woman. Her name was Grushenka. She was beautiful and proud, and both men wanted her — the wild son and the greedy old father. Fyodor even hid a large sum of money, three thousand roubles, to give to Grushenka if she came to him. Dmitri was mad with jealousy.
To make things worse, Dmitri was already promised to another woman, Katerina, who loved him. But Dmitri could not stop thinking about Grushenka.
Dmitri's anger grew and grew. One day, he burst into his father's house in a rage and beat the old man. As he left, he shouted a terrible warning: that he might come back and kill him.
Many people heard these words. Everyone in the town now knew that Dmitri hated his father and had threatened his life.
Chapter 5. A Dangerous Idea.
Meanwhile, Ivan, the cold and clever brother, was troubled by his dark thoughts.

Ivan did not believe in God. And he had reached a frightening conclusion. "If there is no God," he said, "then there is no final judge, and no real right or wrong. And if that is true, then everything is permitted. A man may do anything he wants, even murder, and nothing is truly forbidden."
Ivan said these words as ideas, as philosophy. He did not plan to hurt anyone. But someone was listening very carefully.
Smerdyakov, the strange servant, admired Ivan. He drank in Ivan's words. "Everything is permitted," Smerdyakov thought. "So why not?"

Ivan felt sick of the whole ugly family situation. He decided to leave the town for a while. Before he left, he had a strange, uneasy conversation with Smerdyakov. The servant hinted, in a sly way, that something might happen while Ivan was gone — and that Ivan should leave. Ivan did not fully understand, but a dark feeling followed him as he travelled away.
Without knowing it clearly, Ivan had given Smerdyakov permission. He had planted a poisonous idea in a dangerous mind. And then he had looked away.
Chapter 6. The Night of the Murder.
It was a dark and terrible night.

Dmitri was desperate. He needed money, and he was burning with jealousy over Grushenka. He went to his father's house, sure that Grushenka might be there. He crept into the garden and looked through the window at the old man's greedy face.

For one horrible moment, Dmitri held a heavy tool in his hand and felt hatred fill his heart. He could have done it. But — something stopped him. He did not strike. He ran away from the house into the night, chasing after Grushenka, who was in another place.
But later that night, old Fyodor Karamazov was found dead. Someone had killed him. And the hidden three thousand roubles were gone.

Everything pointed to Dmitri. He had threatened his father. He hated him. He needed money. He had been at the house that very night. He had blood and confusion all over him, and suddenly he had money to spend, though he swore it came from somewhere else.
The police came. They arrested Dmitri for the murder of his father.
Chapter 7. The Wrong Man.
Dmitri swore he was innocent. "I hated my father, yes!" he cried. "I wanted him dead, I admit it! But I did not kill him. I could not do it. At the last moment, I could not!"
No one believed him. The evidence seemed too strong.

Dmitri had lived a wild and foolish life, and now it was destroying him. Yet in prison, something began to change in him. His suffering opened his heart. He started to think about goodness, about God, about the pain of the world. The wild soldier was becoming a deeper man.
Grushenka, who had played with his heart, now saw his true suffering. And her feelings changed into real love. She promised to stay with him, whatever happened.
But the real murderer was still free. And only one person would learn the truth.
Chapter 8. The Truth.
Ivan returned to the town. He could not rest. Something felt terribly wrong. He went to see Smerdyakov, the servant, three times.
At their final meeting, Smerdyakov finally told him the truth. Calmly, coldly, he confessed.
"I killed the old man," Smerdyakov said. "I took the three thousand roubles."
Ivan felt the ground fall away beneath him.

"But you are guilty too," Smerdyakov continued, staring at Ivan. "You taught me that everything is permitted, if there is no God. You wanted him dead, just like your brother did. You went away on purpose, so it could happen. I only did what you believed. You and I did this together."

Ivan was horrified. The murder had grown out of his own words, his own dark ideas. He had not held the weapon, but his philosophy had. Smerdyakov had understood Ivan's cold thoughts better than Ivan himself, and had turned them into blood.
Ivan felt a guilt so heavy he could hardly breathe.
Chapter 9. Ivan's Punishment.
Smerdyakov gave Ivan the stolen money as proof. "Tell the court, if you like," he said. "But no one will believe you. And I will deny it."
That night, Smerdyakov, empty and hopeless, hanged himself. Now the only witness to the truth was dead.

Ivan's mind began to break. His guilt was too great to carry. He became ill with a terrible fever. In his sickness, he saw a frightening vision: he imagined the Devil himself sitting in his room, talking to him, laughing at him, showing him all his own worst thoughts. Ivan's cold, proud mind was falling into darkness. His ideas had destroyed his father and now they were destroying him.
Ivan decided he had to save his innocent brother. He would stand up in court and tell everyone the truth: that Smerdyakov was the killer, and that he, Ivan, was partly to blame.
But he was already very sick. And he had no proof except his own broken words.
Chapter 10. The Trial.
The great day came. The whole region crowded into the courtroom to watch the trial of Dmitri Karamazov. It became famous everywhere.

The lawyers argued. Witnesses spoke. The picture they painted looked bad for Dmitri: the wild son, full of hate, in need of money, who had threatened to kill his father and was there on the night of the murder.
Then Ivan stood up. Shaking with fever and madness, he cried out to the court: "The murderer is not my brother! It was Smerdyakov! And I am guilty too — I told him such things could be done!"

But Ivan looked wild and sick. He shouted about the Devil in his room. To the court, he seemed like a madman, not a witness. No one took his words seriously. His confession only made everything more confused and dramatic.

Katerina, the woman who had loved Dmitri, then did something that destroyed him. To try to protect Ivan, she showed the court an old letter Dmitri had written in a drunken rage, in which he wrote that he might kill his father. This letter seemed like final proof.
The jury went out to decide.
Chapter 11. The Verdict.
The courtroom waited in silence. At last, the jury returned.
"Guilty."
Dmitri was found guilty of murdering his father. He would be sent far away to a hard prison in Siberia for many years.
It was a terrible mistake of justice. The innocent brother was punished, while the true killer was already dead and the guilty thinker walked free but broken.

Yet Dmitri, though crushed, was not the same wild man anymore. His suffering had changed him deeply. "I go for all of us," he said quietly. "I did not kill my father. But I was a bad man, and I accept this suffering. Maybe through pain, I can become new." Grushenka stayed beside him, ready to follow him into exile. There was even a plan, whispered among the family, that Dmitri might escape abroad and start a new life.
Ivan lay ill, fighting for his mind and his soul. His story was left uncertain — a man punished from the inside by his own conscience.
Chapter 12. Love and Hope.
Through all of this darkness, one brother remained a light: Alyosha.

Alyosha loved all of them — wild Dmitri, cold Ivan, even the memory of their cruel father. He did not judge. He carried the words of old Zosima in his heart: that we are all responsible for one another, and that love is stronger than everything.
At the end of the story, Alyosha stood with a group of young boys he had befriended. They had just buried a poor sick child they all loved. The boys were sad and afraid of the future.

Alyosha spoke gently to them. He told them to remember this moment, and to remember their love for one another. "You must know," he said, "that there is nothing higher, stronger, and healthier for life than a good memory, especially a memory from childhood. If a person carries even one good, kind memory in their heart, that memory may one day save them."
The boys listened, their sad faces full of hope. They cheered for Alyosha and for love and for life.

The Karamazov family had been torn apart by greed, jealousy, dark ideas, and murder. But in Alyosha's simple message, Dostoevsky left a door open — a door to forgiveness, to responsibility, and to the healing power of love.
The End.
Chapter 1. The House on the Moors.

High on the wild, windy hills of northern England stood an old, lonely house called Wuthering Heights. The word "wuthering" described the strong, stormy winds that blew across the empty moors around it. It was a hard, cold place, and strange, unhappy things happened there.
Long ago, the house belonged to the Earnshaw family. Mr. Earnshaw had two children: a son named Hindley and a daughter named Catherine.

One day, Mr. Earnshaw went on a journey to the city. When he came back, he brought a surprise with him — a dark-haired orphan boy he had found alone on the streets, with no family and no name. Mr. Earnshaw decided to raise the boy as his own. They called him Heathcliff.
From the very beginning, Hindley hated Heathcliff. He was jealous, because their father seemed to love the strange orphan boy.

But Catherine felt something completely different. She and Heathcliff became close friends almost at once — two wild children, running free across the moors together, laughing in the wind. They were never apart. They belonged to each other.
Chapter 2. Two Wild Hearts.
Catherine and Heathcliff grew up side by side, and their bond grew deeper every year.

They were not gentle, well-behaved children. They were wild and free. They loved to run across the open moors for hours, climbing rocks and racing through the heather, no matter how cold or stormy the weather.
They understood each other completely. It was as if they shared one soul. Catherine was the only person who was kind to Heathcliff, and Heathcliff loved her more than his own life.
But not everyone in the house was happy. Hindley still hated Heathcliff with all his heart. He waited for the day when he could make Heathcliff suffer.
That day came sooner than anyone expected.
Chapter 3. Cruelty.
Old Mr. Earnshaw grew ill, and then he died.
Now Hindley was the master of Wuthering Heights. And Hindley used his new power to punish Heathcliff for all those years of jealousy.
He treated Heathcliff not like a brother, but like a servant. He forced him to work in the fields. He gave him no education and no kindness. He beat him and shamed him whenever he could.
Heathcliff had to bear it all. But inside him, something dark began to grow — a deep, burning anger, and a hunger for revenge. He never forgot a single cruel thing that was done to him.

Only one thing kept him alive through those hard years: his love for Catherine. As long as he had her, he could bear anything. Every evening, they escaped together onto the moors, away from Hindley's cruelty, and they were happy in their own wild world.
But that world was about to change.
Chapter 4. The Other House.

Not far from Wuthering Heights, across the moors, stood a very different house. It was called Thrushcross Grange. It was warm, bright, and beautiful, full of soft carpets and fine things. There lived the Linton family — rich, gentle, and refined.
One day, Catherine hurt her foot near the Grange, and the Lintons took her in to care for her. She stayed with them for several weeks.

When Catherine came back to Wuthering Heights, she had changed. The Lintons had taught her to be a fine, elegant young lady. She wore beautiful dresses now, and had soft manners. She had seen a life of comfort and wealth, and part of her wanted it.
The young man of the Linton family, Edgar, was kind, handsome, and rich. He fell in love with Catherine. And Catherine liked him too — he offered her a soft, respectable, comfortable life.

But her heart still belonged to Heathcliff — poor, dark, wild Heathcliff, who now looked rough and low next to the fine Edgar Linton. Catherine was pulled in two directions, between two very different worlds. And she would have to choose.
Chapter 5. The Choice.
Edgar Linton asked Catherine to marry him. And Catherine said yes.
But her heart was troubled. One evening, she spoke honestly to the housekeeper, not knowing that Heathcliff was listening nearby in the shadows.
"I have agreed to marry Edgar," Catherine said. "It would shame me now to marry Heathcliff. He has no money, no education, nothing. Hindley has made him so low."
Heathcliff heard these words. His heart broke. He turned and slipped away into the night before he could hear the rest.
Because Catherine went on to say something far more important.

"But I do not really love Edgar the way I love Heathcliff," she said. "My love for Edgar is like the leaves on the trees — it will change with time. My love for Heathcliff is like the rocks underneath — deep, and forever. I cannot explain it. He is more myself than I am. Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same. I am Heathcliff."
But it was too late. Heathcliff had already gone. He had heard only that she would be ashamed to marry him. He had not heard that she loved him beyond everything.
That very night, Heathcliff ran away from Wuthering Heights. He disappeared completely. No one knew where he had gone.
Catherine was heartbroken. She searched and waited, but he did not return. In her sadness, she went ahead and married Edgar Linton.
Chapter 6. The Return.
Three years passed. Catherine lived at Thrushcross Grange with Edgar. Her life was calm and comfortable, but a part of her heart was always empty.
Then, one evening, a stranger came to the door. He was a tall, strong, well-dressed gentleman with dark eyes.
It was Heathcliff.

He had come back. And he had changed. In his years away, he had somehow become rich and educated. He looked and spoke like a gentleman now. But his eyes still burned with the same fierce fire — and now, with something colder. He had come back for two reasons: because he could not stay away from Catherine, and because he wanted revenge on everyone who had hurt him.
Catherine was overjoyed to see him. But Edgar, her husband, was worried and jealous. He did not like this dark, powerful man who clearly loved his wife.

Heathcliff began to visit often. And each visit stirred up old feelings and old pain. Catherine was caught, once again, between the two men — the gentle husband she had chosen, and the wild soulmate she had lost.
Chapter 7. Revenge Begins.
Heathcliff's heart was now full of a cold plan for revenge. He wanted to destroy the people who had wronged him and take everything they had.

First, he turned to Hindley, the man who had treated him so cruelly as a boy. Hindley had fallen on hard times. He drank too much and gambled away his money. Heathcliff cleverly lent him money and won his bets, until slowly, Heathcliff gained control of Wuthering Heights itself — the very house where he had once been a servant. Now he was the master.

Then Heathcliff did something cruel to hurt the Linton family. Edgar had a sweet, gentle sister named Isabella. Foolishly, Isabella fell in love with Heathcliff. Heathcliff did not love her at all. But he married her — only to hurt Edgar and to get closer to the Linton money and property.
He treated poor Isabella coldly and unkindly. She soon understood the terrible mistake she had made. Eventually, frightened and unhappy, she ran away from him.
Heathcliff did not care. His heart had room for only two things now: his love for Catherine, and his revenge.
Chapter 8. Catherine's End.
All this trouble and pain was too much for Catherine.

She was torn apart inside — between Edgar and Heathcliff, between the calm life she had chosen and the wild love she could not forget. Her health began to fail. She grew weak and ill, and her mind became troubled.
Catherine was going to have a baby, but she was very sick. Heathcliff came to see her one last time. Their meeting was full of love, anger, and terrible sadness.
"You left me!" he cried. "How could you betray your own heart? You loved me, and yet you married him. You have broken both our hearts."
"We have hurt each other terribly," Catherine wept. "But I cannot live without you, and I cannot live with you. Forgive me."
They held each other, crying, knowing it was the end.
That night, Catherine gave birth to a baby girl — a little daughter, also named Catherine. But the mother, the wild Catherine, died.
When Heathcliff heard that she was dead, he was destroyed. His grief was wild and terrible. He did not want peace or comfort. He wanted her back.
"May you never rest while I live!" he cried into the night. "Haunt me, then! Be with me always — drive me mad — only do not leave me alone in this world without you!"
From that day, Heathcliff was a haunted man. He believed Catherine's spirit was always near him, just out of reach. And his heart grew even colder and darker.
Chapter 9. A Longer Revenge.
Losing Catherine did not stop Heathcliff's revenge. If anything, it made him worse.
He decided to punish not only the people who had hurt him, but their children too. His revenge stretched into the next generation.

When Hindley died, Heathcliff took full control of Wuthering Heights. Hindley had a young son named Hareton — Catherine's nephew. Heathcliff raised the boy exactly as Hindley had once raised him: with no education, no kindness, treated like a rough servant. It was a cold and cruel kind of justice.
Isabella, who had run away from Heathcliff, had given birth to a weak, sickly son named Linton. When Isabella died, Heathcliff took the boy to live with him — not out of love, but to use him.

Heathcliff now had a dark plan. He forced his sickly son, Linton, to marry young Catherine — Edgar's daughter, the child of his lost love. Through this marriage, Heathcliff would take control of both houses and all the family's property.
Soon after, both old Edgar and the sickly young Linton died. Heathcliff had won. He now owned everything — both great houses, all the land, all the money. His revenge was complete.
But he was not happy. He was only empty, and still haunted by Catherine.
Chapter 10. A New Love.
Now, at Wuthering Heights, lived three people: cold, dark Heathcliff; young Catherine, the daughter of his lost love; and Hareton, the rough young man he had raised without kindness.

At first, young Catherine looked down on Hareton. He could not even read. He was rough and awkward, shaped by years of Heathcliff's cruelty. And Hareton felt ashamed next to the clever, educated girl.
But slowly, something changed between them.

Young Catherine began to feel sorry for how she had treated Hareton. She started to teach him to read, gently and patiently. And Hareton, who had never known real kindness, began to soften. They grew close. They began to care for each other. And then, quietly, they fell in love.

It was a love that was healing the old wounds. Where the older generation had known only pain and revenge, these two young people were finding tenderness and hope. Their love was like a small, warm light growing in that cold, dark house.
And strangely, this new love began to affect Heathcliff too.
Chapter 11. The End of Heathcliff.
Heathcliff watched young Catherine and Hareton fall in love. And something happened inside him that he did not expect.
When he looked at them, he saw the ghosts of the past. Young Catherine had her mother's eyes. Hareton reminded him of himself, long ago. Everywhere he looked, he saw his lost Catherine.

Suddenly, all his desire for revenge drained away. What was the point of it now? He had destroyed his enemies, taken everything — and it had brought him no peace at all. The only thing he truly wanted was Catherine, and no revenge could ever bring her back.

Heathcliff began to change. He stopped caring about his plans and his property. He seemed to be looking at something the rest of them could not see. He said he felt Catherine near him, closer than ever — that she was almost within reach.
He stopped eating. He wandered on the moors at night, in the wind and rain, calling her name. He seemed both in terrible pain and strangely full of joy, as if he were close to finally reaching her.
One stormy morning, they found Heathcliff dead in his room, by an open window. The rain had blown in on him. And on his hard face was a strange, peaceful smile.
At last, he was free. At last, he believed, he was with his Catherine again.
Chapter 12. Peace on the Moors.
After Heathcliff died, the darkness lifted from Wuthering Heights.

Young Catherine and Hareton were free now, and free to love each other. They planned to marry. The cruelty and revenge that had ruled two generations were finally over. The old wounds were healed by their gentle, patient love. Where there had been hate, now there was tenderness. Where there had been darkness, now there was light.
They would leave the cold, lonely house behind and live together at bright, warm Thrushcross Grange, and begin a new and happier life.

As for Heathcliff and Catherine — the people who lived nearby began to tell a story. On wild, stormy nights, they said, you could see two figures walking together on the moors, in the wind and the heather. It was Heathcliff and Catherine, together at last, free forever in the wild place they had loved as children.

Their love had been too fierce, too wild for this world. It had brought them, and everyone around them, great suffering. But in death, perhaps, they had finally found the peace they could never find in life.
And on the quiet moors, under the soft grass, the storms of their hearts were finally still.
The End.
